test.ans: If they change only one thing, they know that thing caused any change in the result. If they change many things, they cannot tell which one made the difference.

test.q: Name a weather hazard in California and describe one design that reduces its impact.
test.ans: Sample: Floods. Storm drains carry rainwater away from streets, or levees keep rivers from spilling onto land.

test.q: A school near a creek floods during heavy winter rains. The class compared two solutions. Solution A, a row of sandbags: costs $200, held back water about 30 cm deep in a test, must be set up before every storm. Solution B, a rain garden with plants and gravel: costs $800, soaked up water so the school field stayed dry in 5 of 6 storms, needs weeding twice a year. The school's budget is $1,000 and the principal wants a solution that does not need to be set up before every storm. Make a claim about which solution has more merit for this school. Use evidence from the data and explain your reasoning.
test.ans: Claim: Solution B, the rain garden, has more merit for this school. Evidence: It kept the field dry in 5 of 6 storms, it costs $800, which is under the $1,000 budget, and it only needs weeding twice a year. Sandbags must be set up before every storm. Reasoning: The rain garden meets the criterion of reducing flooding and fits the constraints of the budget and of not needing setup before each storm, so it is the better design solution even though it costs more.
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

units.name: Unit 3: Forces and Motion
units.el: Act out push, pull, balanced and unbalanced with a rope and a cart; have students draw force arrows and label them with "push" or "pull" and "bigger" or "smaller."

lessons.name: What makes an object start or stop moving?

practice.q: A push or a pull is called a
practice.h: It is the word scientists use for any push or pull.

practice.q: A ball is sitting still on the grass. What is needed to make it move?
practice.h: Objects at rest need a push or pull to start moving.

practice.q: A wagon is rolling across the playground. Which force will make it stop?
ch: a pull or push in the opposite direction, like friction from the ground
a push in the same direction
practice.h: To stop something, the force must act against the motion.

practice.q: Which action is a pull?
practice.h: A pull moves something toward you.

practice.q: Ana pushes a toy car and it rolls 85 centimeters. Then she pushes it harder and it rolls 140 centimeters. How many centimeters farther did it roll after the harder push?
practice.h: Subtract the shorter distance from the longer one.

practice.q: Describe what happens to a soccer ball's motion when a player kicks it, and then when the goalie catches it.
practice.ans: The kick is a force that makes the ball start moving. When the goalie catches it, the goalie's hands push against the ball and make it stop.

quiz.q: Which is an example of a force?
A hockey puck slides across the ice and slowly stops. Which force slows it down?
ch: friction between the puck and the ice
a push from the wind behind it

quiz.q: How can you make a rolling ball change direction?
A class rolled a ball 3 times with a gentle push. It rolled 40 cm, 45 cm and 50 cm. How many centimeters did it roll in all?
Jamal kicks a ball softly and then kicks the same ball harder. What happens with the harder kick?
ch: The ball moves faster and goes farther.
The ball goes the same distance.

quiz.q: A toy car rolls farther on a smooth wood floor than on a carpet with the same push. What is the best explanation?
ch: The carpet causes more friction, which slows the car more.
The carpet pushes the car forward.
The wood floor has no gravity.
The car is lighter on wood.

quiz.q: Name two ways a force can change an object's motion. Give an example of each.
quiz.ans: A force can start or stop motion, like kicking a ball or catching it. A force can change direction, like hitting a tennis ball back over the net. (Speeding up or slowing down also count.)

lessons.name: What happens when forces are balanced or unbalanced?

practice.q: When two forces are the same size and push in opposite directions, the forces are
practice.h: Think of a tug of war where no one moves.

practice.q: In a tug of war, Team Red pulls left with a force of 200 newtons and Team Blue pulls right with a force of 200 newtons. What happens to the rope?
practice.h: Compare the two forces.

practice.q: Team Red now pulls left with 250 newtons and Team Blue still pulls right with 200 newtons. Which way does the rope move?
practice.h: The rope moves toward the bigger force.

practice.q: Using the same tug of war (Team Red pulls 250 newtons, Team Blue pulls 200 newtons), how many newtons more does Team Red pull?
practice.h: Find the difference between the two forces.

practice.q: A book is resting on a table. Gravity pulls it down and the table pushes it up. What is true about these forces?
ch: They are balanced, so the book stays still.
They are unbalanced, so the book moves.
There are no forces on the book.
practice.h: The book is not moving. What does that tell you?

practice.q: Draw or describe a force diagram for a box that two children push from opposite sides, where one child pushes harder. Tell which way the box moves.
practice.ans: Two arrows pointing toward each other from opposite sides of the box; the arrow for the harder push is longer. The box moves in the direction of the longer arrow, away from the child who pushes harder.

quiz.q: Unbalanced forces on an object can
In a force diagram, a longer arrow means
Two dogs pull on the same rope toy in opposite directions. The toy does not move. What can you conclude?
ch: The dogs are pulling with equal force.
One dog is pulling much harder.
There are no forces on the toy.
The toy is too heavy for any force.

quiz.q: Mia pushes a box to the right with 30 newtons. Leo pushes it to the left with 18 newtons. How many newtons stronger is Mia's push?
Using the same pushes (Mia pushes right with 30 newtons, Leo pushes left with 18 newtons), which way does the box move?
A box has 40 newtons pushing left and 40 newtons pushing right. What is the difference between the two forces in newtons?

A class tested a cart with two spring scales attached to opposite ends. Trial 1: left pull 5 newtons, right pull 5 newtons, the cart did not move. Trial 2: left pull 5 newtons, right pull 8 newtons, the cart moved right. Trial 3: left pull 9 newtons, right pull 4 newtons, the cart moved left. Make a claim about what makes the cart move. Use evidence from the data and explain your reasoning.
quiz.ans: Claim: The cart moves only when the forces are unbalanced, and it moves toward the stronger pull. Evidence: In trial 1 the pulls were equal (5 and 5) and the cart stayed still. In trial 2 the right pull was stronger (8 vs 5) and the cart moved right. In trial 3 the left pull was stronger (9 vs 4) and it moved left. Reasoning: Balanced forces cancel each other, so motion does not change. Unbalanced forces change the cart's motion in the direction of the bigger force.
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

lessons.name: How can we predict motion that repeats?

practice.q: Which motion repeats in a pattern?
ch: a child swinging back and forth on a swing
a rock sitting on the ground
a leaf landing once on the grass
a ball resting in a box
practice.h: Look for something that keeps going back and forth.

practice.q: A pendulum is a weight hanging from a string that swings back and forth. A class counts its swings: 10 swings in the first 10 seconds and 10 swings in the next 10 seconds. How many swings should it make in the next 10 seconds?
practice.h: Use the pattern the class already saw.

practice.q: A pendulum makes 12 swings every 10 seconds. How many swings will it make in 30 seconds?
practice.h: 30 seconds is three groups of 10 seconds.

practice.q: A ball is dropped and bounces. Each bounce is lower than the one before. Which prediction fits the pattern?
ch: The next bounce will be lower again.
The next bounce will be higher.
The ball will bounce forever at the same height.
practice.h: What happened each time it bounced?

practice.q: A seesaw goes up and down when two children take turns pushing off the ground. Why can you predict when one side will go up?
ch: The motion repeats in a regular pattern.
There is no force on it.
practice.h: Think about what happens over and over.

practice.q: A student times a swing. It goes forward and back 4 times every 10 seconds. Explain how the student can use this pattern to predict the number of swings in 20 seconds.
practice.ans: The pattern shows 4 swings every 10 seconds. 20 seconds is two 10-second groups, so it should make about 4 + 4 = 8 swings.

quiz.q: Patterns in motion help us
A class tested pendulums with different string lengths. Short string: 15 swings in 15 seconds. Long string: 9 swings in 15 seconds. What pattern does the data show?
ch: The longer string swings more slowly.

quiz.q: Using the same data (short string 15 swings, long string 9 swings in 15 seconds), how many more swings did the short string make?
A toy car rolls down a ramp, up a small hill and back down, again and again on a curved track. A student wants to predict where the car will be. What should the student do first?
ch: observe and record where it goes several times to find a pattern

quiz.q: A playground swing goes back and forth 3 times every 6 seconds. How many times will it go back and forth in 12 seconds?
A pendulum is pulled back and let go. It makes a regular pattern of swings. A student wants it to swing more slowly. Based on what the class learned, what should the student change?
Give an example of a motion in everyday life that repeats in a pattern and explain how you could use it to make a prediction.
quiz.ans: Sample: A playground swing moves back and forth at a steady pace. If I count 5 swings every 10 seconds, I can predict about 10 swings in 20 seconds.

test.q: A force is
ch: a kind of energy you can see
the weight of an object only

test.q: Which force slows down a bike when the rider squeezes the brakes?
Forces that are equal in size and opposite in direction are
A shopping cart is still. A child pushes it with a small force. What happens?
ch: The cart starts to move in the direction of the push.

test.q: Two students pull a box in opposite directions with the same force. What happens to the box?
ch: It moves toward the first student.
It moves toward the second student.

test.q: In a force diagram, an arrow pointing right is longer than an arrow pointing left. What will the object do?
Which change will make a rolling marble stop sooner?
ch: rolling it onto a rough carpet

test.q: Team A pulls a rope with 320 newtons. Team B pulls the other way with 290 newtons. How many newtons stronger is Team A's pull?
Using the same tug of war (Team A pulls 320 newtons and Team B pulls 290 newtons), which team will win?
A pendulum swings 8 times every 10 seconds. How many times will it swing in 40 seconds?
A ball rolls toward a wall and bounces back. What caused its direction to change?
ch: The wall pushed on the ball.
The ball ran out of energy.

test.q: A book sits on a shelf without moving. Which is true?
ch: The forces on it are balanced.
The forces on it are unbalanced.
Only one force acts on it.

test.q: A class pushed a toy truck with a weak, medium and strong push. Distances: weak 30 cm, medium 70 cm, strong 120 cm. What pattern does the data show?
ch: A stronger push makes the truck go farther.
A stronger push makes the truck go a shorter distance.
All pushes made the truck go the same distance.

test.q: Using the same data (weak 30 cm, medium 70 cm, strong 120 cm), how many centimeters farther did the truck go with the strong push than the weak push?
Using the same data (weak 30 cm, medium 70 cm, strong 120 cm), what is the total distance for all three pushes?
Two pendulums are the same except for string length. Pendulum A has a 20 cm string and Pendulum B has a 60 cm string. Which prediction is best?
ch: Pendulum B will swing more slowly.
Pendulum A will swing more slowly.
Both will swing at exactly the same rate.
Pendulum B will not swing at all.

test.q: A cart is pulled left with 6 newtons and right with 6 newtons. Then the right pull changes to 10 newtons. What happens?
ch: The cart starts moving to the right.
The cart starts moving to the left.
The cart moves up and down.

test.q: Which is an example of motion with a pattern you can predict?
ch: the hands moving around a clock
a paper bag blowing in a gusty wind
a dropped puzzle piece sliding on the floor
a cat jumping around the room

test.q: A student wants to test whether a harder push makes a ball roll farther. Which must stay the same in every trial?
Explain the difference between balanced and unbalanced forces. Give an example of each.
test.ans: Balanced forces are equal and opposite, so they cancel and the motion does not change, like a lamp sitting on a table. Unbalanced forces are not equal, so they change motion, like kicking a ball to make it move.

test.q: A swing goes back and forth 5 times in 10 seconds. Predict how many times it will swing in 30 seconds and explain your thinking.
test.ans: About 15 times. The swing repeats in a pattern: 30 seconds is three groups of 10 seconds, and 5 + 5 + 5 = 15.

test.q: Describe how you would plan a fair investigation to find out whether a heavier box needs a bigger push to start moving.
test.ans: Use two boxes that are the same size and on the same floor, one with more weight inside. Pull each one with a spring scale and record the force needed to start it moving. Repeat 3 times and compare.

test.q: A class rolled a toy car down the same ramp onto three surfaces. Distance traveled after the ramp: tile floor 210 cm, wood floor 180 cm, carpet 60 cm. Make a claim about how the surface affects the car's motion. Use evidence from the data and explain your reasoning.
test.ans: Claim: Rougher surfaces make the car stop sooner. Evidence: The car went 210 cm on smooth tile and 180 cm on wood, but only 60 cm on carpet, which is the roughest surface. Reasoning: Friction is a force that pushes against motion. The rough carpet causes more friction, so the forces on the car are unbalanced against its motion sooner, which slows it down and stops it in a shorter distance.
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

units.name: Unit 4: Magnets and Static Electricity
units.el: Give partners real magnets, paper clips and a balloon; teach "attract" with a pulling-together hand motion and "repel" with a pushing-apart motion, and use the frame "The ___ attracts/repels the ___ because ___."

lessons.name: How can a magnet move something without touching it?

practice.q: Which object will a magnet attract?
practice.h: Magnets attract objects that contain iron, like steel.

practice.q: A magnet pulls a paper clip toward it before they touch. What does this show?
ch: Magnetic force can act without touching.
The paper clip is pushing itself.
practice.h: Notice that there was a gap between them.

practice.q: A student puts a sheet of paper between a magnet and a paper clip. The clip still moves toward the magnet. What can the student conclude?
ch: Magnetic force can pass through paper.
The paper clip is made of paper.
practice.h: What happened even with the paper in the way?

practice.q: Which is the best question to test with a magnet and a pile of objects?
ch: Which materials does a magnet attract?
practice.h: A good science question can be answered by testing.

practice.q: A class tested 12 objects. The magnet attracted 5 of them. How many objects were not attracted?
practice.h: Subtract the attracted objects from the total.

practice.q: Name two objects in your classroom a magnet would attract and two it would not. Tell what the attracted objects have in common.
practice.ans: Attracted: a steel paper clip and a steel staple. Not attracted: a plastic ruler and a wooden pencil. The attracted objects contain iron or steel.

quiz.q: Most objects that a magnet attracts contain
A student sorts objects. Which group shows only objects a magnet attracts?
ch: steel nail, steel paper clip, iron washer
aluminum foil, glass marble, steel nail

quiz.q: A magnet picked up 6 paper clips on the first try, 8 on the second and 7 on the third. How many paper clips did it pick up in all?
A magnet is held under a thin wooden table. A steel ball on top of the table moves when the magnet moves. Why?
ch: The magnetic force passes through the wood.
The ball is made of wood.

quiz.q: Which is a cause and effect relationship?
ch: Bringing a magnet near a steel pin causes the pin to move.

quiz.q: A student finds that a magnet attracts a steel can but not an aluminum can. Which question would be best to investigate next?
ch: Which other metals does a magnet attract?
How many cans are in the store?

quiz.q: Describe an investigation to find out if a magnet can pull a paper clip through water.
quiz.ans: Put a paper clip in a cup of water. Hold a magnet against the outside of the cup near the clip and move it. Watch whether the clip moves with the magnet.

lessons.name: Why do magnets sometimes push each other away?

practice.q: The two ends of a bar magnet are called
practice.h: They are labeled N and S.

practice.q: What happens when the north pole of one magnet is brought near the south pole of another magnet?
practice.h: Opposite poles behave differently from like poles.

practice.q: What happens when two north poles are brought close together?
practice.h: Poles that are the same push apart.

practice.q: A magnet holds a paper clip when they are 1 cm apart but not when they are 5 cm apart. What does this show?
ch: Magnetic force gets weaker as distance increases.
Magnetic force gets stronger with distance.
practice.h: Compare what happened at the short and long distances.

practice.q: A magnet attracted a paper clip from 4 cm away. A stronger magnet attracted it from 11 cm away. How many centimeters farther away did the stronger magnet work?
practice.h: Subtract the distances.

practice.q: Two ring magnets on a pencil float apart instead of touching. Explain why.
practice.ans: The magnets are placed with the same poles facing each other, so they repel and push each other apart even though they are not touching.

quiz.q: Opposite poles of two magnets

A class measured how many paper clips a magnet could hold through different numbers of index cards. 0 cards: 10 clips. 2 cards: 6 clips. 4 cards: 3 clips. 6 cards: 1 clip. What pattern does the data show?
ch: As the distance grows, the magnet holds fewer clips.
As the distance grows, the magnet holds more clips.
The cards make the magnet stronger.
The number of clips never changes.

quiz.q: Using the same data (0 cards: 10 clips, 6 cards: 1 clip), how many fewer clips did the magnet hold with 6 cards than with 0 cards?
Using the same data (0 cards: 10, 2 cards: 6, 4 cards: 3, 6 cards: 1), predict the number of clips with 8 cards.
Two toy trains have magnets on their ends. When Kai pushes them together, they push apart. What must be facing each other?
ch: like poles, such as north and north

quiz.q: A student says, "A bigger magnet is always stronger." What would be the best way to test this claim?
ch: Test magnets of different sizes and count how many paper clips each one holds.
Look at the colors of the magnets.
Ask a friend which magnet looks strongest.

quiz.q: Explain how you could find out which end of an unlabeled magnet is the north pole, using a magnet that is labeled N and S.
quiz.ans: Bring the labeled north pole near one end of the unlabeled magnet. If they repel, that end is a north pole. If they attract, that end is a south pole.

lessons.name: What makes a balloon stick to a wall?

practice.q: When you rub a balloon on your hair, the balloon gets
practice.h: This is called static electricity.

practice.q: After a balloon is rubbed on hair, the hair stands up and moves toward the balloon. What does this show?
ch: Electric charges can attract without touching.
The hair is made of iron.
practice.h: Was the balloon touching the hair when the hair moved?

practice.q: Two balloons are both rubbed on a wool sweater. When they hang near each other, they push apart. Why?
ch: They have the same kind of charge, so they repel.
They have opposite charges, so they attract.
practice.h: Like charges act like like poles.

practice.q: Which is an example of static electricity?
ch: a shock when you touch a doorknob after walking on carpet
a ball rolling down a hill
practice.h: Think of a tiny spark or a zap.

practice.q: A charged balloon picked up 14 tiny bits of paper. After 5 minutes it could only pick up 6 bits. How many fewer bits did it pick up?
practice.h: Subtract to compare.

practice.q: How are static electricity and magnetism alike?
practice.ans: Both can push or pull objects without touching them, and both can attract and repel.

quiz.q: Static electricity can make objects
A rubbed plastic comb is held near a thin stream of water from a faucet. The water bends toward the comb. What caused this?
ch: the electric charge on the comb

quiz.q: Which question asks about a cause and effect relationship with static electricity?
ch: Does rubbing a balloon longer make it pick up more paper bits?

quiz.q: A class rubbed a balloon for different times. 5 rubs: 3 paper bits. 10 rubs: 7 paper bits. 20 rubs: 15 paper bits. How many more paper bits did 20 rubs pick up than 5 rubs?
Using the same data (5 rubs: 3 bits, 10 rubs: 7 bits, 20 rubs: 15 bits), what pattern do you see?
ch: More rubbing picked up more paper bits.
More rubbing picked up fewer paper bits.

quiz.q: Two balloons rubbed on hair hang near each other. Then one balloon is touched to a metal pole and loses its charge. What will most likely happen?
ch: The balloons stop pushing apart as much.

quiz.q: A student rubbed a balloon on a wool cloth and held it 1 cm, 5 cm and 10 cm above a pile of paper bits. At 1 cm it picked up 12 bits, at 5 cm it picked up 4 bits, and at 10 cm it picked up 0 bits. Make a claim about how distance affects the electric force. Use evidence from the data and explain your reasoning.
quiz.ans: Claim: The electric force gets weaker as the distance gets bigger. Evidence: The balloon picked up 12 bits at 1 cm, 4 bits at 5 cm and 0 bits at 10 cm. Reasoning: The balloon picked up fewer bits as it moved farther away, which means its pull was weaker. The charge can attract without touching, but only when objects are close enough.
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

lessons.name: How can we use magnets to solve a problem?

practice.q: Which everyday object uses a magnet to stay closed?
practice.h: Think of a kitchen door that seals by itself.

practice.q: A recycling center needs to separate steel cans from aluminum cans. Which design idea uses magnets?
ch: Pass the cans under a big magnet that lifts out the steel cans.
practice.h: Which cans does a magnet attract?

practice.q: A class wants to design a latch that keeps a cabinet door closed. Which is a criterion?
ch: The door must stay shut when a small child pulls gently.
It must be finished by Friday.
Only magnets and tape can be used.
practice.h: A criterion tells what the design must do.

practice.q: A magnet latch costs $4. The class needs latches for 6 cabinets. How many dollars will the latches cost?
practice.h: Multiply the cost by the number of cabinets.

practice.q: A student designs a game where a paper fish with a steel paper clip is picked up by a magnet on a string. Why does the game work?
ch: The magnet attracts the steel clip.
practice.h: Which part of the fish does a magnet attract?

practice.q: Describe a problem at home or school that a magnet could help solve, and explain how.
practice.ans: Sample: Pins fall on the floor in the art room. A magnet on a stick could pick up the steel pins quickly without anyone touching the sharp points.

quiz.q: Which problem could a magnet help solve?
ch: finding a steel needle dropped in the carpet

quiz.q: A team designs a magnetic pencil holder for a steel whiteboard. In testing, it slides down when it is full of pencils. What is the best next step?
ch: Use a stronger magnet or add a second magnet and test again.

quiz.q: In a test, a magnet held 9 pencils. A stronger magnet held 15 pencils. How many more pencils did the stronger magnet hold?

A team tests three magnets for a door latch. Magnet A held the door shut against a pull of 2 newtons, Magnet B against 5 newtons, and Magnet C against 9 newtons. The door must stay shut against a pull of at least 4 newtons, and it must open with a pull of 6 newtons or less so adults can open it easily. Which magnet is the best choice?
Why did Magnet A not meet the criterion in that test (it held against only 2 newtons, and the door needed 4 newtons)?
ch: It was too weak to keep the door shut.

quiz.q: A latch design uses 2 magnets. The class is building 7 latches. How many magnets do they need?
Explain how engineers use magnets in at least one real machine or object.
quiz.ans: Sample: Cranes at a scrap yard use giant electromagnets to lift heavy pieces of steel and drop them where they are needed.

test.q: A magnet will attract
The ends of a magnet are called
What happens when the south pole of one magnet faces the south pole of another?
A paper clip jumps up to a magnet before touching it. What does this show?
ch: Magnets can pull objects without touching them.
Paper clips can jump on their own.

test.q: A magnet works through a plastic folder to move a steel pin. What does this show about magnetic force?
A balloon rubbed on hair sticks to a wall. Which force holds it there?
Two balloons rubbed on wool hang near each other. What will they most likely do?
A class measured how far a magnet could pull a paper clip across a table. Small magnet: 2 cm. Medium magnet: 5 cm. Large magnet: 9 cm. Which conclusion is supported?
ch: In this test, larger magnets pulled the clip from farther away.
All magnets have the same strength.
Paper clips pull on magnets more than magnets pull on clips.

test.q: Using the same data (small magnet 2 cm, large magnet 9 cm), how many centimeters farther did the large magnet pull the clip than the small magnet?
A magnet held 3 steel washers on Monday, 4 on Tuesday and 5 on Wednesday. How many washers did it hold in all?
Which question can be answered by an investigation with magnets?
ch: Does the magnet's pull get weaker when it is farther from a paper clip?

test.q: A recycling machine uses a magnet to pull out some cans. Which cans does it remove?
Which pair shows two objects that can attract each other without touching?
ch: a balloon rubbed on hair and small bits of paper
a wooden block and a plastic cup
a glass jar and a cotton ball

test.q: A charged comb picked up 10 bits of paper at 1 cm and 3 bits at 4 cm. How many fewer bits did it pick up at 4 cm?
A magnet holds 12 clips with no cards between it and the clips, 7 clips through 3 cards and 2 clips through 6 cards. Which is the best prediction for 9 cards?
A student wants to know whether magnets work through water. Which investigation is best?
ch: Put a steel clip in a cup of water and move a magnet outside the cup to see if the clip moves.
Put a magnet in water and see if it floats.
Hold a magnet above an empty cup.

test.q: A team designs a magnetic sign holder that falls off a steel door during testing. What should the team do?
ch: find why it failed and improve the design, then test again
test it on a wooden door

test.q: Which design solution uses magnets to solve a problem?
ch: a cabinet latch that keeps a door shut without a lock
a rubber band that holds papers
a glue stick that holds a poster
a nail that holds a picture

test.q: A team needs 3 magnets for each sign holder. How many magnets do they need for 8 sign holders?
Explain how magnetism and static electricity are different.
test.ans: Magnets attract objects made of iron or steel and have north and south poles. Static electricity comes from charges made by rubbing materials, and it can attract light objects like paper, hair or water.

test.q: Write a cause and effect question about magnets and describe how you would test it.
test.ans: Sample: Does adding more paper between a magnet and a paper clip make the pull weaker? Add one sheet of paper at a time and count how many clips the magnet can still hold.

test.q: A class tested how the distance between a magnet and a steel paper clip affects the pull. They used a spring scale to measure the force needed to pull the clip away. 1 cm: 6 units of force. 2 cm: 4 units. 3 cm: 2 units. 4 cm: 1 unit. Make a claim about how distance affects magnetic force. Use evidence from the data and explain your reasoning.
test.ans: Claim: Magnetic force gets weaker as the distance between the magnet and the clip increases. Evidence: At 1 cm it took 6 units of force to pull the clip away, but at 4 cm it took only 1 unit. The force went down each time the distance went up. Reasoning: A magnet can pull on steel without touching, but the pull depends on how close the objects are, so the closer the clip, the stronger the magnetic force.
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

units.name: Unit 5: Life Cycles and Inherited Traits
units.el: Use picture cards of each life-cycle stage for sequencing with "first, next, then, last"; build a two-column chart "inherited from parents" and "changed by the environment" with photos.

lessons.name: Do all living things have the same life cycle?

practice.q: Which shows the stages of a butterfly's life cycle in order?
practice.h: Start with the stage that hatches.

practice.q: What do all life cycles have in common?
practice.h: Think about what happens to every living thing.

practice.q: A young frog that lives in water and breathes with gills is called a
practice.h: This stage has a tail and no legs at first.

practice.q: Which is a stage in the life cycle of a bean plant?
practice.h: Which word describes a young plant that just sprouted?

practice.q: A monarch egg hatched after 4 days. The caterpillar ate and grew for 14 days. Then it was a chrysalis for 10 days. How many days passed from egg to adult?
practice.h: Add all three stages.

practice.q: Draw or describe a model of a plant's life cycle. Label at least four stages.
practice.ans: A circle with arrows: seed, seedling (sprout), adult plant, flower, fruit with new seeds, and back to seed.

quiz.q: The stage when an animal makes offspring is called
How is a frog's life cycle like a butterfly's life cycle?
ch: The young look very different from the adults.

quiz.q: A chicken hatches from an egg as a chick, grows into an adult hen and lays eggs. Which stage is missing from this description of its life cycle?
Grasshoppers hatch as small nymphs that look like tiny adults without wings. How is this different from a butterfly?
ch: Grasshoppers have no caterpillar or chrysalis stage.

quiz.q: A tomato seed sprouted in 7 days. The plant grew for 50 more days before its first flower. How many days after planting did the first flower appear?
A frog egg took 6 days to hatch. The tadpole stage lasted 70 days. How many more days was the tadpole stage than the egg stage?
Compare the life cycle of a frog with the life cycle of a dog. Name one way they are alike and one way they are different.
quiz.ans: Alike: both are born, grow, reproduce and die. Different: a frog hatches from an egg as a tadpole that looks different from the adult, but a puppy is born alive and looks like a small adult dog.

lessons.name: Why do offspring look like their parents?

practice.q: A trait passed from parents to offspring is called
practice.h: "Inherit" means to get something from your parents.

practice.q: Which is an inherited trait in a dog?
ch: knowing how to sit on command
practice.h: Which one was the dog born with?

practice.q: Two black cats have a litter of kittens. Some kittens are black and one is gray. What does this show?
ch: Offspring can vary even though they inherit traits from their parents.
Kittens never look like their parents.
practice.h: Variation means differences among members of a group.

practice.q: A litter of 7 puppies has 4 puppies with spots. How many puppies do not have spots?
practice.h: Subtract the spotted puppies from the total.

practice.q: Which trait of a sunflower is inherited from the parent plants?
ch: a broken stem from the wind
a tag a gardener tied on it
a bite taken by a rabbit
practice.h: Which trait comes from the plant's parents and not from something that happened to it?

practice.q: Describe two traits you could observe to show that a baby rabbit is related to its parents.
practice.ans: Sample: The shape of its long ears and the color of its fur are similar to its parents' traits.

quiz.q: Offspring usually look
ch: similar to their parents, but not exactly the same
exactly the same as their parents
like a different kind of animal

quiz.q: A class measured the ear length of 5 rabbits from the same parents: 9 cm, 10 cm, 8 cm, 10 cm and 9 cm. What does the data show?
ch: The rabbits have similar but not identical ear lengths.
All rabbits have the same ear length.

quiz.q: Using the same data (9 cm, 10 cm, 8 cm, 10 cm, 9 cm), how many centimeters longer is the longest ear than the shortest ear?
A farmer wants pea plants with purple flowers. Which plants should the farmer use to make seeds?
Which trait is NOT inherited?
ch: a child's ability to ride a bike

quiz.q: A tally of 20 puppies in a dog show found 12 with floppy ears and the rest with pointed ears. How many puppies had pointed ears?
Explain why brothers and sisters in the same family can look different from each other.
quiz.ans: They each inherit a different mix of traits from their two parents, so they show variation even though they are related.

lessons.name: Can the environment change an organism's traits?

practice.q: Two plants grew from seeds of the same parent. One grew in a sunny window and is tall and green. One grew in a dark closet and is short and pale. What caused the difference?
ch: the environment, because of the amount of light
practice.h: The seeds came from the same parent. What was different?

practice.q: Flamingos get their pink color from pigments in the food they eat. A flamingo in a zoo is given food without these pigments. What will most likely happen?
ch: Its new feathers will be paler.
practice.h: The color comes from the food.

practice.q: Which trait is caused by the environment?
ch: strong arm muscles from swimming every day
the shape of a person's nose
practice.h: Which one changed because of something the person did?

practice.q: A plant in rich soil grew 32 cm. A plant from the same seed packet in poor soil grew 19 cm. How many centimeters taller was the plant in rich soil?
practice.h: Subtract the heights.

practice.q: A dog inherits a body built for running fast. Its owner never lets it exercise, so it becomes slow and out of shape. What does this show?
ch: Traits can be affected by both inheritance and the environment.
Running speed has nothing to do with the body.
The dog did not inherit any traits.
Exercise changes a dog's fur color.
practice.h: Think about what the dog was born with and what happened to it.

practice.q: Give one example of a trait in a plant that can be changed by the environment, and explain how.
practice.ans: Sample: A plant's height can change. If it gets less water or light than it needs, it grows shorter than it would in good conditions.

quiz.q: Which trait of a tree is most affected by its environment?
ch: how tall it grows, depending on water and sun
the kind of seeds it makes
the type of bark it has

quiz.q: A class grew bean plants from the same seed packet. Group A got 50 mL of water a day and grew 18 cm. Group B got 10 mL of water a day and grew 6 cm. Which conclusion is supported?
ch: The amount of water affected how tall the plants grew.

quiz.q: Using the same data (Group A grew 18 cm and Group B grew 6 cm), how many centimeters taller was Group A?
In a plant investigation, Group A got 50 mL of water a day. How many milliliters did Group A get in 7 days?
Hydrangea flowers can be blue in some soils and pink in other soils. What does this tell you?
ch: Soil, a part of the environment, can affect flower color.
Hydrangeas inherit their color only from their parents.

quiz.q: Two puppies from the same litter have very similar inherited traits. One lives where it gets lots of food and exercise, and one gets very little food. Years later, one is much bigger. What is the best explanation?
ch: The environment, especially food, affected their size.
Dogs grow bigger with less food.
Size is never affected by food.

quiz.q: A gardener planted seeds from the same sunflower in two places. Place 1: full sun, plants grew an average of 180 cm. Place 2: mostly shade, plants grew an average of 90 cm. Make a claim about what caused the difference in height. Use evidence and explain your reasoning.
quiz.ans: Claim: The amount of sunlight in the environment caused the difference in height. Evidence: The seeds came from the same parent plant, but plants in full sun grew about 180 cm while plants in shade grew about 90 cm. Reasoning: The plants inherited similar traits, so the difference must come from the environment. Plants need light to make food and grow, so less light meant shorter plants.
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

test.q: Which stage comes right after the egg in a butterfly's life cycle?
Which is an inherited trait of a person?
All living things are born, grow, reproduce and
Which animal's young look very different from the adults?
Which list shows the life cycle of a flowering plant in order?
ch: seed, seedling, adult plant, flower, new seeds

test.q: A baby giraffe has a long neck like its parents. This trait is
Kittens in one litter have different fur colors. This is an example of
Which of these traits was caused by the environment and not inherited?
ch: a plant leaning toward the window it grows beside
the number of legs on a spider
the shape of a bird's beak

test.q: A parrot learns to say "hello." Is this an inherited trait?
ch: No, it was learned from the environment.
Yes, all parrots are born saying "hello."
Yes, its parents taught it in the egg.

test.q: A ladybug egg hatches in 4 days, the larva stage lasts 16 days and the pupa stage lasts 7 days. How many days from egg to adult?
A pea plant made 48 seeds. A gardener planted 30 of them. How many seeds were not planted?
A class measured the height of 4 corn plants grown from seeds of the same parents in the same garden: 150 cm, 155 cm, 148 cm, 152 cm. What does the data show?
ch: Plants from the same parents show small differences, called variation.
The plants have very different parents.
The plants are all exactly the same.
Corn plants do not inherit traits.

test.q: Using the same data (150 cm, 155 cm, 148 cm, 152 cm), how many centimeters taller is the tallest plant than the shortest plant?
Flamingos fed food without pink pigments grow paler feathers. What is the cause of the paler feathers?
ch: their diet, which is part of the environment

test.q: Two cuttings from the same rose bush are planted. Cutting A gets good soil and water and makes 20 flowers. Cutting B gets poor soil and little water and makes 4 flowers. Which statement is best supported?
ch: The environment affected the number of flowers.
Poor soil makes roses grow more flowers.
Water has no effect on roses.

test.q: Using the same data (Cutting A made 20 flowers and Cutting B made 4 flowers), how many flowers did they make in all?
A model of a frog's life cycle is drawn as a circle with arrows. Why is it drawn as a circle?
ch: Adults make eggs, so the cycle starts again.
The frog stops at the adult stage.

test.q: Which pair of offspring and parents shows inherited traits?
ch: a puppy with spots like its mother
a child who learned to swim from a coach
a plant that grew tall in the sun

test.q: Which stage is part of a grasshopper's life cycle but not a butterfly's?
Explain how a frog's life cycle and a bean plant's life cycle are alike and different.
test.ans: Alike: both begin small (an egg or a seed), grow, reproduce and die. Different: the frog changes from a tadpole that lives in water to an adult with legs, while the bean grows from a seed into a plant that makes flowers and seeds.

test.q: Explain why a person's height can be affected by both inherited traits and the environment.
test.ans: A person can inherit traits for being tall or short from their parents, but things in the environment like healthy food and sleep also affect how tall they grow.

test.q: A student says, "If I cut my hair short, my children will be born with short hair." Explain why this is wrong.
test.ans: A haircut is a change caused by the environment, not an inherited trait. Changes like a haircut are not passed to offspring, so the children's hair will follow inherited traits.

test.q: Two goldfish came from the same parents. Goldfish A lived in a large tank and grew to 15 cm long. Goldfish B lived in a small, crowded bowl and grew to only 6 cm long. Both got the same kind of food. Make a claim about why the goldfish are different sizes. Use evidence and explain your reasoning.
test.ans: Claim: The environment, the size and crowding of the home, caused the difference in size. Evidence: Both goldfish had the same parents and the same food, but the fish in the large tank grew to 15 cm and the fish in the small, crowded bowl grew to only 6 cm. Reasoning: Because the fish inherited traits from the same parents, the big difference in size is best explained by their different environments. A crowded, small space limited how much Goldfish B could grow.
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

units.name: Unit 6: Survival, Groups and Fossils
units.el: Show photos of animal groups and fossils with captions; pre-teach habitat, survive, camouflage, fossil and advantage, and use the frame "The ___ helps the ___ survive because ___."

lessons.name: Why do some animals live in groups?

practice.q: A large group of fish swimming together is called a
practice.h: It is the same word as a place where you learn.

practice.q: How does living in a pack help wolves?
ch: They can hunt large animals together.
They can fly to find food.
practice.h: Think about what is hard for one wolf to do alone.

practice.q: In a beehive, some bees collect food, some care for young and some guard the hive. What is the benefit?
ch: Dividing the jobs helps the whole group survive.
Each bee has to do everything.
It keeps the bees from making honey.
practice.h: What happens when everyone has a job?

practice.q: Emperor penguins huddle close together in the Antarctic winter. Why?
ch: to share body heat and stay warm
practice.h: Antarctica is extremely cold.

practice.q: A herd has 23 adult elephants and 9 young elephants. How many elephants are in the herd?
practice.h: Add the adults and the young.

practice.q: Name one animal that lives in a group and describe one way the group helps it survive.
practice.ans: Sample: Meerkats live in groups. While some meerkats look for food, one stands guard and warns the others when a predator comes.

quiz.q: Which is a benefit of living in a group?
ch: being easier for predators to find alone

quiz.q: Small fish swim in a tight school. How might this help them when a large fish attacks?
ch: It is harder for the predator to catch just one fish.
The predator gets lost in the sand.
The small fish turn into rocks.

quiz.q: Which is a cost, or problem, of living in a big group?
A scientist counted zebras in a herd on two days. Day 1: 48 zebras. Day 2: 57 zebras. How many more zebras were counted on Day 2?
A scientist observed that a lion hunting alone caught prey 2 out of 10 tries. Lions hunting in a group caught prey 5 out of 10 tries. What does this data suggest?
ch: Hunting in a group helped the lions catch prey more often.

quiz.q: Using the same data (alone: 2 catches out of 10 tries, group: 5 catches out of 10 tries), how many more catches did the group make?

Scientists watched a group of birds called crows. When crows fed alone, a hawk caught one about every 5 days. When crows fed in a flock of 20 with lookouts, a hawk caught one about every 30 days. Make a claim about whether living in a group helps crows survive. Use evidence and explain your reasoning.
quiz.ans: Claim: Living in a group helps crows survive. Evidence: Crows feeding alone were caught about every 5 days, but crows in a flock of 20 were caught only about every 30 days. Reasoning: In a group, lookouts can see a hawk coming and warn the others, so fewer crows are caught and more of them survive.
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

lessons.name: How do an animal's traits help it survive?

practice.q: Fur, feathers or color that helps an animal blend in with its surroundings is called
practice.h: It helps an animal hide.

practice.q: A white rabbit and a brown rabbit live in a snowy field. Which one is more likely to be seen by a fox?
practice.h: Which color stands out against the snow?

practice.q: Some male birds have brighter feathers than others of the same kind. How can this trait help them?
ch: Bright feathers can help them attract mates and reproduce.
Bright feathers help them hide from all predators.
Bright feathers make them fly slower.
practice.h: Survival also means having offspring.

practice.q: A scientist put 20 green and 20 brown paper "beetles" on green grass. Birds found 15 brown beetles and 4 green beetles. How many beetles did the birds find in all?
practice.h: Add the brown and green beetles found.

practice.q: Using the same beetle data (birds found 15 brown and 4 green beetles on green grass), which trait was an advantage on green grass?
practice.h: Which color was found less often?

practice.q: Explain how a cactus's spines are a trait that helps it survive.
practice.ans: The spines protect the cactus from animals that might eat it for its water and food.

quiz.q: A trait that helps an organism survive and reproduce is
Giraffes with longer necks can reach leaves high in trees. During a dry season with few low leaves, which giraffes are most likely to survive?
Some plants make fruit that animals like to eat. The animals carry the seeds away in their droppings. How does this help the plant?
ch: Its seeds spread to new places to grow.
It keeps the plant from making flowers.

quiz.q: In a field, 50 moths were dark and 50 were light. A month later there were 38 dark moths and 21 light moths left. How many more dark moths survived than light moths?
Using the same moth data (38 dark moths and 21 light moths left), what is the most likely reason?
ch: The dark moths were harder for birds to see in that field.
The light moths flew away to a better place.

quiz.q: Among a group of deer, some can run a little faster than others. A pack of wolves moves into the area. What will most likely happen over many years?
ch: More of the faster deer will survive and have offspring.
The slower deer will become faster right away.
All the deer will stop running.

quiz.q: Explain why small differences in traits among animals of the same kind can make a difference in survival.
quiz.ans: Some differences, like a better color for hiding or longer legs for running, give certain animals an advantage. Those animals are more likely to survive, find mates and have offspring.

lessons.name: What happens when a habitat changes?

practice.q: A habitat is
ch: the place where an organism lives and gets what it needs
a stage in a life cycle
practice.h: It is an organism's home.

practice.q: Which animal can survive well in a hot, dry desert?
ch: a camel that can go a long time without drinking
a polar bear with thick fur
a fish that breathes with gills
a seal that hunts in icy water
practice.h: Which animal has traits for little water and high heat?

practice.q: A pond dries up during a long drought. Which organisms will have the hardest time surviving?
ch: birds that can fly to a new pond
deer that can walk to a river
practice.h: Which organisms cannot leave the water?

practice.q: A wetland had 64 frogs before it was drained to build a road. Afterward, scientists counted 15 frogs. How many fewer frogs were there?
practice.h: Subtract the new count from the old count.

practice.q: A forest is cut down and the land becomes a grassy field. Which animal is most likely to do well in the new habitat?
ch: a woodpecker that nests in trees
a squirrel that stores nuts in trees
practice.h: Which animal needs grass instead of trees?

practice.q: Explain why some organisms survive well in a habitat, some survive less well and some cannot survive at all.
practice.ans: Each organism has traits that fit certain conditions. If the habitat gives it what it needs, it survives well. If it gets only some of what it needs, it survives less well. If its needs are not met, it cannot survive there.

quiz.q: A shallow ocean habitat gets much warmer. Coral that needs cool water begins to die. Fish that hide in the coral also become fewer. Why did the fish decrease?
ch: They lost the coral they need for shelter.

quiz.q: A town wants to build homes on a field where a rare butterfly lives. Which solution best helps both the town and the butterfly?
ch: build on part of the field and protect the part with the plants the butterflies need
move all the butterflies to the Arctic

quiz.q: Data from a stream: before a factory opened, the stream had 40 trout. Two years later it had 12 trout, and the water was much warmer. Which claim is supported?
ch: The warmer water made the stream less fit for trout.

quiz.q: Using the same stream data (40 trout before and 12 trout two years later), how many fewer trout were in the stream?
Volunteers planted 35 native plants on Saturday and 47 on Sunday to rebuild a habitat. How many plants did they plant?

A class compared two ways to help salmon in a river with a dam. Plan A: build a fish ladder so salmon can swim past the dam. Plan B: paint the dam green. Which plan has more merit for helping salmon reach their spawning grounds?
ch: Plan A, because it gives salmon a path past the dam
Plan B, because green is a natural color
neither plan, because salmon do not swim upstream

quiz.q: Describe one change to a habitat caused by people and one solution that could reduce its harm to living things.
quiz.ans: Sample: Building a highway cuts a forest in two so animals cannot reach food. A wildlife bridge over the highway lets animals cross safely.

lessons.name: What can fossils tell us about the past?

practice.q: A fossil is
ch: the remains or traces of a living thing from long ago
practice.h: Fossils can be bones, shells, footprints or imprints.

practice.q: A fossil of a fern is found in a place that is now very cold and icy. What does this suggest?
ch: The place was once warmer and wetter.
The fossil is from the future.
practice.h: Ferns need warm, moist places to grow.

practice.q: Fossils of fish and seashells are found in rock on a dry hilltop. What can you infer?
ch: The area was once covered by water.
Birds dropped the fish there last week.
practice.h: Where do fish and shells live?

practice.q: The La Brea Tar Pits in Los Angeles hold fossils of mammoths, saber-toothed cats and dire wolves. What do these fossils tell us?
ch: Animals that no longer live there once lived in that area.
Those animals still live in Los Angeles today.
The animals are only made-up stories.
practice.h: Are mammoths alive in Los Angeles now?

practice.q: A museum has 27 mammoth bones and 19 saber-toothed cat bones on display. How many bones are on display in all?
practice.h: Add the two numbers.

practice.q: Explain how a dinosaur footprint fossil can give information even though it is not a bone.
practice.ans: The footprint shows the size and shape of the dinosaur's foot, how many toes it had and that it walked over soft mud in that place.

quiz.q: Which is a trace fossil?
ch: a fresh seashell from the beach

quiz.q: A fossil shows a large animal with a body like an elephant and long curved tusks. Which modern animal is it most similar to?
Fossils of palm trees are found in a place that now has cold winters with snow. What is the best explanation?
ch: The climate there was warmer long ago.
Palm trees grow best in snow.
Someone buried the palm trees last year.
The fossils are made of snow.

quiz.q: A fossil layer is 75 centimeters below the ground. A deeper fossil layer is 130 centimeters below the ground. How many centimeters deeper is the second layer?
Which question can fossils help scientists answer?
ch: What kinds of organisms lived in this place long ago?
What will the weather be tomorrow?
How many people live here today?
What is the name of this town?

quiz.q: Fossils of a sea animal are found in the bottom rock layer of a cliff, and fossils of land plants are found in a layer above it. What is the best interpretation?
ch: The area was once under the sea and later became land.
Sea animals climbed onto the land plants.
The plants lived under the sea.

quiz.q: Describe what a fossil of an animal that is now extinct can tell us.
quiz.ans: It shows what the animal looked like, how big it was and what kind of environment it lived in, even though no living animals of that kind exist today.

test.q: The place where an organism lives and gets food, water and shelter is its
Which is a fossil?
ch: the shape of a shell pressed into rock
a live crab on the beach
a rock shaped like a heart

test.q: Why do zebras live in large herds?
ch: Many eyes can spot predators and warn the group.
Herds make it easier to find snow.

test.q: A green grasshopper lives in a green meadow. How does its color help it survive?
ch: It blends in so birds have trouble seeing it.
It helps it make food from sunlight.

test.q: Which organism would survive least well in a hot, dry desert?
ch: a fern that needs moist soil
a lizard that hides in the shade
a kangaroo rat that gets water from seeds

test.q: Fossils of corals are found in a mountain far from the ocean. What does this show?
ch: The land was once under warm ocean water.
Coral can live on dry mountains.
Corals are a kind of tree.

test.q: Ants work together to carry a large leaf back to their nest. What does this show?
ch: Working in a group helps them get food.
Leaves are light for one ant.

test.q: A river is dammed and the area below the dam gets much less water. What will most likely happen to fish that live below the dam?
ch: The fish will grow legs and walk.

test.q: A park had 84 quail. After a wildfire burned their bushes, there were 37 quail. How many fewer quail were there?
Students counted 18 ladybugs on Monday, 26 on Tuesday and 14 on Wednesday in the school garden. How many ladybugs did they count in all?
Light-colored mice and dark-colored mice live on dark lava rock. Which mice will owls most likely catch more often?
ch: neither, because owls do not eat mice

test.q: A scientist found 60 light mice and 60 dark mice on dark rock at the start of the year. At the end of the year, there were 14 light mice and 52 dark mice. How many more dark mice than light mice survived?
Using the same mouse data (14 light mice and 52 dark mice at the end of the year), how many mice survived in all?
Which statement best explains the mouse data?
ch: Dark fur was an advantage on dark rock, so more dark mice survived.
Light mice are faster than dark mice.
Fur color does not affect survival.

test.q: The La Brea Tar Pits have fossils of mammoths and camels. These animals no longer live in Los Angeles. What can scientists conclude?
ch: The animals living in that area have changed over time.
Mammoths still live in Los Angeles.

test.q: A forest habitat is replaced by a shopping center. Which solution would most help forest animals?
ch: keep a strip of forest connecting the remaining woods
cut down the rest of the forest
pave the parking lot with dark asphalt

test.q: Plants in a rain forest have large, broad leaves. Plants in a desert have small, waxy leaves or spines. What is the best explanation?
ch: Each plant has traits that fit the conditions of its habitat.
Rain forest plants are a different color.

test.q: A fossil-hunting club found 13 shell fossils, 8 plant fossils and 5 fish fossils. How many fossils did they find in all?
Animals that live in a group and hunt together, like lions, are called a
Explain one way living in a group helps animals survive and one way it can make survival harder.
test.ans: Helps: the group can protect each other from predators or hunt together. Harder: the animals must share food and water, and diseases can spread through the group.

test.q: Fossils of tropical plants are found in a place that now has cold winters. Explain what this tells you about the environment long ago.
test.ans: The environment used to be much warmer, because tropical plants need warm temperatures to grow. The climate in that place has changed over a long time.

test.q: A wetland was partly drained for farmland. Scientists counted animals before and after. Frogs: 120 before, 30 after. Ducks: 45 before, 20 after. Field mice: 15 before, 40 after. Make a claim about how draining the wetland affected these animals. Use evidence from the data and explain your reasoning.
test.ans: Claim: Draining the wetland helped some animals survive and made it harder for others. Evidence: Frogs dropped from 120 to 30 and ducks dropped from 45 to 20, but field mice rose from 15 to 40. Reasoning: Frogs and ducks need water to live, find food and reproduce, so they survived less well when the water was removed. Field mice live in dry fields, so the new dry habitat gave them more of what they need.
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

sci|4.about: Fourth graders investigate energy: how speed relates to energy, what happens in collisions, and how energy moves by sound, light, heat and electric current. They design devices that convert energy, study natural resources, model waves and the way light lets us see, explore how plant and animal structures and senses support survival, and read rock layers and landforms to explain how Earth's surface changes and how people reduce the impact of natural hazards.
std: Use evidence to construct an explanation relating the speed of an object to the energy of that object.
Make observations to provide evidence that energy can be transferred from place to place by sound, light, heat and electric currents.
Apply scientific ideas to design, test and refine a device that converts energy from one form to another.
Develop a model of waves to describe patterns in terms of amplitude and wavelength and that waves can cause objects to move.
Construct an argument that plants and animals have internal and external structures that function to support survival, growth, behavior and reproduction.
Identify evidence from patterns in rock formations and fossils in rock layers to support an explanation for changes in a landscape over time.
Obtain and combine information to describe that energy and fuels are derived from natural resources and their uses affect the environment.
Generate and compare multiple solutions to reduce the impacts of natural Earth processes on humans.

units.name: Unit 1: Energy, Speed and Collisions
units.el: Model the words speed, energy, collide and transfer with toy cars and a ramp; post the frames "The faster ___, the more ___" and "When ___ hit ___, energy moved from ___ to ___."

lessons.name: Why does a faster object have more energy?

practice.q: An object that is moving has
practice.h: Anything that moves has a kind of energy.

practice.q: Two identical balls roll across the floor. Ball A rolls faster than Ball B. Which has more energy of motion?
practice.h: Compare their speeds.

practice.q: A class rolled a marble down a ramp from different heights and timed it over 1 meter of floor. Higher starting points made the marble move faster. Why?
ch: Starting higher gave the marble more energy, so it moved faster.
practice.h: Think about what the height gave the marble before it was released.

practice.q: A marble rolled 1 meter in 4 seconds from a low ramp and 1 meter in 2 seconds from a high ramp. How many seconds faster was the high-ramp roll?
practice.h: Subtract the times.

practice.q: A soccer ball is kicked softly and then kicked hard. Evidence that the hard kick gave it more energy is that it
ch: moved faster and knocked over more cones
practice.h: What can a faster ball do that a slower ball cannot?

practice.q: Explain how you could tell which of two rolling toy cars has more energy without touching them.
practice.ans: Measure or compare their speeds. The faster car has more energy. I could also see which car pushes a cup farther when it hits it.

quiz.q: The faster an object moves, the
A bowling ball rolls slowly and knocks down 2 pins. The same ball rolls quickly and knocks down 9 pins. What does this evidence show?
ch: The faster ball had more energy to transfer to the pins.
The pins were heavier the first time.
Speed and energy are not related.

quiz.q: Using the same data (the slow roll knocked down 2 pins and the fast roll knocked down 9 pins), how many more pins did the fast roll knock down?
A class released a cart from heights of 10 cm, 20 cm and 30 cm. The cart pushed a block 5 cm, 11 cm and 16 cm. What pattern does the data show?
ch: Higher release heights made the cart push the block farther.
Higher release heights made the cart push the block a shorter distance.

quiz.q: Using the same data (the block moved 5 cm, 11 cm and 16 cm), how many centimeters did the block move in all three trials?
A bike rider stops pedaling and coasts. As the bike slows down, what is happening to its energy of motion?
Write an explanation that relates the speed of a thrown baseball to its energy. Use the words faster and energy.
quiz.ans: A baseball thrown faster has more energy. That is why a fast pitch makes a louder smack in the glove and is harder to stop than a slow pitch.

lessons.name: What happens to energy when objects collide?

practice.q: When two objects run into each other, it is called a
practice.h: Think of bumper cars.

practice.q: A rolling marble hits a still marble. The first marble slows down and the second marble starts moving. What happened?
ch: Energy moved from the first marble to the second marble.
The second marble made new energy.
practice.h: Where did the second marble get its energy?

practice.q: A moving toy car crashes into a block, and you hear a loud bang. Into what forms did some of the car's energy change?
ch: sound and heat, plus motion of the block
practice.h: What did you hear and what moved?

practice.q: A cart moving at 60 cm per second hits a wall and bounces back at 25 cm per second. How many centimeters per second slower is it moving after the collision?
practice.h: Subtract the speed after from the speed before.

practice.q: In a game of pool, a cue ball hits another ball. Which question asks about energy changes in this collision?
ch: How does the speed of the cue ball change after it hits the other ball?
What color is the cue ball?
How old is the pool table?
practice.h: Energy changes show up as changes in speed.

practice.q: Describe what happens to the energy in a collision between a rolling ball and a row of dominoes.
practice.ans: The ball's energy of motion moves to the first domino, which falls and transfers energy to the next one. Some energy also becomes sound and a little heat.

quiz.q: In a collision, energy can be
ch: transferred from one object to another
kept only by the faster object

quiz.q: A soccer player kicks a ball. Which statement best describes the energy?
ch: Energy moved from the player's foot to the ball.
The ball created its own energy.
The foot gained energy from the ball.

quiz.q: Two toy cars collide. Before the crash, Car A moved fast and Car B was still. After the crash, Car A moved slowly and Car B moved forward. Which claim is supported?
ch: Some of Car A's energy was transferred to Car B.
Car B had more energy before the crash.
Energy was destroyed in the crash.

quiz.q: A marble rolled 120 cm when nothing was in its path. When it hit a paper cup, the cup moved 30 cm and the marble stopped after 45 cm. How many centimeters shorter was the marble's roll when it hit the cup?
A car crash test shows that a car going 20 km per hour causes small damage and a car going 60 km per hour causes much more damage. What is the best explanation?
ch: The faster car has more energy to transfer in the collision.
Faster cars are made of weaker metal.
Speed has no effect on energy.

quiz.q: A cart hit a block 4 times and pushed it 12 cm, 14 cm, 13 cm and 13 cm. How many centimeters did it push the block in all?

A class rolled a ball down a ramp into a cup from three heights. Height 10 cm: cup moved 6 cm. Height 20 cm: cup moved 13 cm. Height 30 cm: cup moved 19 cm. Make a claim about how speed affects the energy transferred in a collision. Use evidence and explain your reasoning.
quiz.ans: Claim: A faster ball transfers more energy in a collision. Evidence: The ball from 10 cm moved the cup 6 cm, from 20 cm 13 cm and from 30 cm 19 cm. Reasoning: Releasing the ball from higher makes it roll faster. A faster ball has more energy, so when it hits the cup it transfers more energy and pushes the cup farther.
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

lessons.name: Where does the energy go after a crash?

practice.q: When you clap your hands, the energy of your moving hands changes partly into
practice.h: What do you hear?

practice.q: Rubbing your hands together quickly makes them feel warm. What does this show?
ch: Motion energy can change into heat.
practice.h: Notice the warmth.

practice.q: A falling apple hits the ground and stops. Where did most of its energy go?
ch: into sound, heat and moving the ground a tiny bit
practice.h: Energy is never destroyed. Think about what you would hear and feel.

practice.q: A car's bumper is tested in a crash. At 10 km per hour, a sensor records 15 units of sound. At 30 km per hour, it records 48 units. How many more units of sound were recorded at 30 km per hour?
practice.h: Subtract the smaller reading.

practice.q: Why do helmets have foam inside?
ch: The foam takes in some of the energy of a collision so less reaches your head.
Foam adds energy to a crash.
practice.h: Think about what foam does when it is squeezed.

practice.q: A car brakes and stops. Explain where the car's energy of motion goes.
practice.ans: The brakes rub against the wheels, and friction changes the energy of motion into heat. A little energy also becomes sound.

quiz.q: Energy cannot be
A hammer hits a nail. Which shows that energy was changed into other forms?
ch: The nail gets slightly warm and you hear a bang.
The nail turns a new color.

quiz.q: Two identical balls are dropped onto a floor from different heights. The ball dropped from higher makes a louder sound. Why?
ch: It was moving faster and had more energy when it hit.

quiz.q: A ball dropped from 100 cm bounced back to 65 cm. How many centimeters lower was the bounce than the drop height?
Using the same ball (dropped from 100 cm, bounced to 65 cm), why did it not bounce all the way back to 100 cm?
ch: Some energy changed into sound and heat when it hit the floor.

quiz.q: A class dropped a ball 3 times and measured bounces of 60 cm, 62 cm and 64 cm. What is the average bounce height in centimeters? (Add the trials and divide by 3.)
Explain why a car moving at 50 km per hour is more dangerous in a crash than the same car moving at 20 km per hour. Use the word energy.
quiz.ans: The faster car has more energy of motion. In a crash that energy is transferred to whatever it hits and changes into sound, heat and damage, so more energy means more damage.

test.q: An object's energy of motion depends on its
When two objects bump into each other, it is a
Energy can change from one form to another, but it cannot be
A skateboarder goes faster and faster down a hill. What is happening to the skateboarder's energy of motion?
A moving bowling ball hits pins. The ball slows down and the pins fly. What does this show?
ch: Energy was transferred from the ball to the pins.
The pins had energy before they were hit.

test.q: You hear a crunch when a cart hits a wall. What does the sound show?
ch: Some of the cart's energy changed into sound.

test.q: Which ball has the most energy?
ch: a ball thrown at 30 meters per second
a ball thrown at 10 meters per second
a ball rolling at 2 meters per second

test.q: A class rolled a toy car down ramps of three heights and measured how far it pushed a box: low 8 cm, middle 17 cm, high 25 cm. Which conclusion is supported?
ch: The car had more energy when it started higher and moved faster.
Low ramps give the most energy.
The box gave energy to the car.

test.q: Using the same data (low 8 cm, middle 17 cm, high 25 cm), how many centimeters farther did the box move from the high ramp than the low ramp?
Using the same data (low 8 cm, middle 17 cm, high 25 cm), what is the total distance the box moved in all three tests?
Why do race cars have crumple zones that fold in a crash?
ch: They take in energy of the crash so less reaches the driver.

test.q: A cue ball hits a still pool ball straight on. After the hit, the cue ball almost stops and the other ball rolls away. Where did the cue ball's energy mostly go?
Which question would help you investigate how speed affects energy?
ch: Does a faster rolling ball knock over more blocks?
How many people own a ball?

test.q: A cart moving at 80 cm per second hits a block and slows to 35 cm per second. By how many centimeters per second did it slow down?
A ball was dropped 4 times. The bounces were 50 cm, 54 cm, 52 cm and 48 cm. What is the average bounce height in centimeters? (Add the trials and divide by 4.)
A truck and a bicycle both travel at the same speed and each hits a parked bin. The truck knocks the bin much farther. Which is the best explanation?
ch: The heavier truck had more energy at the same speed.
The bin was lighter when the bicycle hit it.
Speed is the only thing that affects energy.

test.q: Two students roll the same ball at a wall. Student A's ball makes a loud thump. Student B's ball makes a quiet tap. What can you infer?
ch: Student A rolled the ball faster.
Student B rolled the ball faster.
Both rolled it at the same speed.

test.q: Rubbing two sticks together quickly can make them hot. What energy change is this?
A rolling marble slows down and stops on carpet. Where did its energy go?
ch: It changed mostly into heat from friction with the carpet.
It went back into the marble's color.

test.q: Explain why a faster-moving baseball can knock a can off a fence when a slow one cannot.
test.ans: The faster baseball has more energy. When it hits the can, it transfers more energy, enough to push the can off the fence.

test.q: A ball dropped from 2 meters bounces back only 1 meter. Explain what happened to the rest of its energy.
test.ans: When the ball hit the ground, some of its energy changed into sound and heat and some moved into the ground, so less energy was left to lift the ball back up.

test.q: Students tested how speed affects energy. They launched a cart at three speeds into a foam block and measured how deep a dent it made. Slow: 2 mm. Medium: 5 mm. Fast: 9 mm. Make a claim about how speed relates to energy. Use evidence and explain your reasoning.
test.ans: Claim: A faster-moving object has more energy. Evidence: The slow cart made a 2 mm dent, the medium cart 5 mm and the fast cart 9 mm. Reasoning: Making a deeper dent takes more energy. The cart transferred its energy to the foam in the collision, so the faster cart must have had more energy to transfer.

Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
