units.name: Unit 2: Energy Transfer, Electricity and Design
units.el: Build a class chart of energy forms (motion, sound, light, heat, electrical) with icons; give students arrow cards to model conversions such as "electrical -> light" and the frame "The ___ changes ___ energy into ___ energy."

lessons.name: How does energy travel from place to place?

practice.q: Sunlight warms a sidewalk. Which form of energy traveled from the Sun to the sidewalk?
practice.h: What travels from the Sun to Earth through space?

practice.q: A metal spoon is placed in a cup of hot soup. Soon the handle feels hot. What happened?
ch: Heat moved from the soup through the spoon.
Cold moved from the spoon into the soup.
The spoon made its own heat.
practice.h: Heat moves from warmer things to cooler things.

practice.q: You hit a drum and a nearby paper scrap on a second drum jumps. What does this show?
ch: Sound carries energy from place to place.
practice.h: Something made the paper move without touching it.

practice.q: A cup of cocoa was 80°C. After 15 minutes it was 52°C. How many degrees did it cool?
practice.h: Subtract the ending temperature from the starting temperature.

practice.q: Which is an example of energy moving by electric current?
ch: a wire carrying energy from a battery to a bulb
a ball rolling down a hill
practice.h: Electric current moves through wires.

practice.q: Give two examples from your home of energy moving from one place to another. Name the form of energy in each.
practice.ans: Sample: Heat moves from a stove burner to a pot. Light moves from a lamp to my book so I can read. Electricity moves through a cord to a TV.

quiz.q: Which can carry energy from place to place?
ch: sound, light, heat and electric current

quiz.q: Two cans of water sat in the sun for 1 hour. The can painted black warmed from 20°C to 34°C. The can painted white warmed from 20°C to 26°C. Which claim is supported?
ch: The black can took in more energy from sunlight.
The white can took in more energy.
The cans made their own heat.

quiz.q: Using the same data (black can 20°C to 34°C, white can 20°C to 26°C), how many more degrees did the black can warm than the white can?
A loud truck passes and the windows in a house rattle. Which energy reached the windows?
An ice cube is held in a warm hand and melts. Which way did heat move?
ch: from the hand to the ice
from the ice to the hand
from the air into the ice and then into the hand

quiz.q: A lamp is 3 meters from a solar cell. Moving it closer increases the reading from 12 units to 30 units. How many units did the reading increase?
Describe an investigation to show that light carries energy.
quiz.ans: Place two thermometers in the same spot, one in sunlight and one shaded by a box. After 20 minutes, compare temperatures. The thermometer in light will be warmer, showing light carried energy to it.

lessons.name: How does electricity move through a circuit?

practice.q: A complete path that electricity can flow through is called a
practice.h: The path must have no gaps.

practice.q: Which material is a good conductor of electricity?
practice.h: Conductors let electricity flow easily. Most metals are conductors.

practice.q: A bulb is connected to a battery with two wires, but one wire is not touching the battery. What happens?
ch: The bulb does not light because the circuit is open.
practice.h: Is there a complete loop?

practice.q: Why are electric wires covered with plastic or rubber?
ch: These insulators keep electricity from flowing where it should not.
They make the wire conduct better.
practice.h: Insulators block the flow of electricity.

practice.q: A class tested 14 objects in a circuit. The bulb lit for 6 objects. How many objects did not light the bulb?
practice.h: Subtract the objects that lit the bulb from the total.

practice.q: Draw or describe a simple circuit that lights a bulb. Explain why it works.
practice.ans: A battery, two wires and a bulb connected in a loop from one end of the battery, through the bulb and back to the other end. It works because the closed loop lets electric current carry energy from the battery to the bulb.

quiz.q: What does a switch do in a circuit?
ch: opens or closes the path for electricity

quiz.q: A student tests objects in a circuit. The bulb lights for a steel nail, a foil strip and a brass key. It stays dark for an eraser and a craft stick. Which conclusion is supported?
ch: Metals tested were conductors; the eraser and stick were insulators.

quiz.q: A flashlight does not work. The batteries are new. What is a likely cause?
ch: There is a gap in the circuit, such as a loose connection.
The batteries have too much energy.
The switch is made of metal.

quiz.q: A circuit uses 3 batteries. Each battery is 1.5 volts. How many volts do the batteries give together?
In a circuit, energy moves from the battery to a buzzer. What energy change happens at the buzzer?
A battery-powered fan ran for 45 minutes on Monday and 70 minutes on Tuesday. How many minutes did it run in all?
Explain the difference between a conductor and an insulator and give one example of each.
quiz.ans: A conductor lets electricity flow through it easily, like copper. An insulator does not let electricity flow easily, like rubber or plastic.

lessons.name: How can we change energy from one form to another?

practice.q: A solar panel changes
practice.h: Solar panels work in sunlight.

practice.q: An electric fan changes electrical energy mostly into
practice.h: What do the blades do?

practice.q: A speaker changes electrical energy into
practice.h: What do you hear from a speaker?

practice.q: A flashlight battery stores energy. When the flashlight is on, the energy changes into
practice.h: Touch an old-style bulb after it has been on a while.

practice.q: A small motor lifted a paper clip 40 cm with 1 battery and 95 cm with 2 batteries. How many centimeters higher did it lift the clip with 2 batteries?
practice.h: Subtract the heights.

practice.q: Name a device in your home and describe the energy change it makes.
practice.ans: Sample: A toaster changes electrical energy into heat that browns the bread.

quiz.q: Which device changes motion energy into electrical energy?
A hand-crank flashlight lights when you turn the handle. Which shows the energy changes in order?
Which device changes electrical energy into heat?
A wind turbine turns in the wind and lights the houses in a town. What energy change happens in the turbine?
ch: motion energy of the wind becomes electrical energy

quiz.q: A solar charger charged a phone 20 percent in the morning, 35 percent at midday and 15 percent in the afternoon. How many percent did it charge in all?
A class tested a rubber-band car. 2 winds: 60 cm. 4 winds: 120 cm. 6 winds: 180 cm. How many centimeters did the car travel for each wind?
Explain how a person riding a bike with a light powered by the wheel changes energy from one form to another.
quiz.ans: The rider's moving legs give motion energy to the wheel. A small generator on the wheel changes that motion energy into electrical energy, and the bulb changes it into light.

lessons.name: How do engineers design and improve an energy device?

practice.q: A class must build a solar oven that warms a cracker to at least 40°C using a pizza box, foil and plastic wrap. The temperature goal is a
practice.h: It describes what success looks like.

practice.q: A class must build a solar oven using only a pizza box, foil and plastic wrap. The rule "only a pizza box, foil and plastic wrap" is a
practice.h: It limits the materials.

practice.q: Why would a team line its solar oven with foil?
ch: Foil reflects more sunlight into the oven.
practice.h: Think about what shiny surfaces do with light.

practice.q: The team's oven heated from 22°C to 47°C. How many degrees did the temperature rise?
practice.h: Subtract the starting temperature from the ending temperature.

practice.q: A solar oven test was done on a sunny day, and the improved oven was tested on a cloudy day. What is wrong with comparing these results?
ch: The weather changed, so the test was not fair.
Ovens work better on cloudy days.
The oven should be tested at night.
practice.h: What else changed besides the design?

practice.q: List two criteria and one constraint for a device that changes motion into sound, such as an alarm that rings when a door opens.
practice.ans: Criteria: it must make a sound loud enough to hear across the room; it must make sound every time the door opens. Constraint: it must cost less than $5, or it must use only materials from the classroom.

quiz.q: Three solar oven designs were tested at the same time on the same day. Design A reached 38°C, Design B 51°C and Design C 45°C. The goal was at least 40°C. Which designs met the criterion?
Using the same data (Design A 38°C, B 51°C, C 45°C), how many degrees hotter did Design B get than Design A?
Design B used black paper and plastic wrap. Design C used black paper but no plastic wrap. What can the team learn by comparing them?
ch: how the plastic wrap affected the temperature
how the color of the box mattered

quiz.q: Design C reached 45°C in three tests: 44°C, 45°C and 46°C. What was the average? (Add the trials and divide by 3.)
Design B works best, but its plastic wrap tears easily. What should the team do next?
ch: improve the wrap part and test again under the same conditions

quiz.q: Two alarm designs both ring when a door opens. Alarm 1 costs $3 and is loud enough to hear across the room. Alarm 2 costs $12 and is a little louder. The budget is $5 per alarm. Which alarm is the better solution?
ch: Alarm 1, because it meets the criteria and the budget
neither, because alarms do not use energy

quiz.q: A team tested two wind turbine blade designs with the same fan at the same distance. Design 1 (2 blades) made the bulb light for 5 seconds per 10 seconds of wind. Design 2 (4 blades) made the bulb light for all 10 seconds. Make a claim about which design better converts wind energy into electrical energy. Use evidence and explain your reasoning.
quiz.ans: Claim: Design 2 with 4 blades converts wind energy into electrical energy better. Evidence: With the same fan and distance, Design 2 kept the bulb lit for all 10 seconds, while Design 1 lit it only 5 seconds. Reasoning: The test was fair because the fan and distance stayed the same. The bulb lit longer, which shows more motion energy from the wind was changed into electrical energy by Design 2.
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

test.q: Which form of energy travels from the Sun to Earth?
ch: motion of air from the Sun

test.q: Which material is an insulator?
A battery, wires and a bulb connected in a complete loop form a
A pot of water sits on a hot stove. Heat moves
ch: from the stove to the pot and water
from the water to the stove
only from the air to the pot

test.q: Which device changes electrical energy into light?
A student plucks a rubber band and nearby rice grains on a box bounce. What carried energy to the rice?
In a circuit, the bulb goes out when a student opens the switch. Why?
ch: The path is broken, so current cannot flow.
The battery ran out of energy instantly.

test.q: Which energy change happens in a solar-powered calculator?
A class tested materials in a circuit. The bulb lit with a paper clip, a key and foil. It did not light with a rubber band, a crayon or a cotton ball. Which object would most likely light the bulb?
A metal spoon in hot water warmed from 21°C to 48°C. How many degrees did it warm?
A flashlight uses 4 batteries. Each battery is 1.5 volts. How many volts in all?
A solar oven was tested 3 times and reached 54°C, 58°C and 50°C. What was the average temperature? (Add the trials and divide by 3.)
Which pair names a device and its energy change correctly?
A team is building a device that lights a bulb when a door opens. Which is a constraint?
ch: It may use only one battery.
It must light the bulb every time.
It must be bright enough to see.
It must work when the door opens.

test.q: Three alarms were tested in the same room. Alarm X was heard 4 meters away, Alarm Y 9 meters away and Alarm Z 6 meters away. The criterion is "heard at least 5 meters away." Which alarms meet the criterion?
Using the same data (Alarm X 4 meters, Alarm Y 9 meters, Alarm Z 6 meters), how many meters farther was Alarm Y heard than Alarm X?
A team's solar oven reached 35°C on a cloudy day. They added foil flaps and tested it again on a sunny day, and it reached 55°C. Why can't they be sure the foil flaps caused the change?
ch: The weather also changed, so it was not a fair test.

test.q: A wind turbine model produces less electricity than planned. Which next step follows the engineering design process?
ch: find the part that is not working well, change it and test again
change all the parts at once and skip testing

test.q: Why does a black shirt feel warmer than a white shirt in sunlight?
ch: Black takes in more light energy and changes it to heat.
Black shirts make their own heat.

test.q: Explain how energy moves through a circuit to light a bulb.
test.ans: Stored energy in the battery moves as electric current through the wires to the bulb, where it changes into light and heat. The circuit must be closed for current to flow.

test.q: Describe one device that changes energy from one form to another and name the forms of energy before and after.
test.ans: Sample: A hand-crank radio changes motion energy from turning the crank into electrical energy, and then the speaker changes it into sound.

test.q: Students tested which cup keeps cocoa hot longest. They poured 70°C cocoa into three cups and measured the temperature after 20 minutes. Thin paper cup: 41°C. Plastic cup: 47°C. Foam cup with lid: 62°C. Make a claim about which cup is best at keeping heat from moving out. Use evidence from the data and explain your reasoning.
test.ans: Claim: The foam cup with a lid is best at keeping heat in. Evidence: After 20 minutes, the cocoa in the foam cup was still 62°C, compared with 47°C in plastic and 41°C in paper. The foam cup lost only 8 degrees, while the paper cup lost 29 degrees. Reasoning: Heat moves from the hot cocoa to the cooler air. The foam and lid slow that transfer of energy, so the cocoa stayed hotter. The paper cup let heat move out the fastest.
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

units.name: Unit 3: Natural Resources and Energy Use
units.el: Sort picture cards of resources (sun, wind, coal, oil, river, wood) into "renewable" and "nonrenewable"; pre-teach fuel, resource, pollution and renewable with student-friendly definitions and examples.

lessons.name: Where does the energy we use come from?

practice.q: A natural resource is
ch: something from nature that people use
something made only in a factory
practice.h: It comes from Earth, not from people.

practice.q: Coal, oil and natural gas are called fossil fuels because they formed from
ch: remains of living things from millions of years ago
practice.h: Think about what "fossil" means.

practice.q: How does a power plant that burns natural gas make electricity?
ch: Burning the gas makes heat that boils water into steam, and the steam spins a generator.
The gas glows like a bulb.
The gas freezes and makes current.
practice.h: Follow the energy from burning to spinning.

practice.q: Which natural resource is used to make electricity at a hydroelectric dam?
practice.h: "Hydro" means water.

practice.q: A town gets its electricity from three sources: 45 percent natural gas, 35 percent solar and the rest from wind. What percent comes from wind?
practice.h: All the parts add up to 100 percent.

practice.q: Choose one energy source and explain where its energy originally comes from.
practice.ans: Sample: Wind energy comes from moving air. The Sun heats Earth's surface unevenly, which makes air move as wind.

quiz.q: Which is a fuel that comes from a natural resource?
Wood is burned in a fireplace to warm a room. What energy change happens?
ch: stored energy in the wood changes into heat and light

quiz.q: A wind farm has turbines on hills where it is often windy. Why are turbines placed there?
ch: Strong, steady wind turns the blades more, making more electricity.

quiz.q: A wind turbine made 120 units of electricity on Monday and 85 units on Tuesday. How many units did it make in both days?
A solar farm makes 900 units of electricity on a sunny day and 350 units on a cloudy day. How many fewer units does it make on a cloudy day?
Which energy resource depends on sunlight to work?
Explain how a fossil fuel like oil is a natural resource even though people pump it out of the ground.
quiz.ans: Oil formed naturally over millions of years from the remains of ancient living things. People only collect it and process it into fuels like gasoline.

lessons.name: Which energy resources will run out?

practice.q: A renewable resource is one that
ch: can be replaced naturally in a short time
will be used up and never replaced
practice.h: "Renew" means to make new again.

practice.q: Which is a nonrenewable energy resource?
practice.h: Which takes millions of years to form?

practice.q: Why will we eventually run out of oil if we keep using it?
ch: It takes millions of years to form, much longer than we use it.
Oil is made by the Sun each day.
practice.h: Compare how fast it forms with how fast we use it.

practice.q: A school used 1,200 units of electricity in March and 950 units in April after turning off unused lights. How many units did the school save?
practice.h: Subtract April from March.

practice.q: Which list has only renewable resources?
practice.h: Check each item in the list.

practice.q: Sort these into renewable and nonrenewable: wind, coal, sunlight, natural gas. Explain one of your choices.
practice.ans: Renewable: wind and sunlight. Nonrenewable: coal and natural gas. Coal is nonrenewable because it took millions of years to form and cannot be replaced quickly.

quiz.q: Which energy resource is renewable?
Trees can be replanted after they are cut for firewood. What kind of resource is wood when forests are replanted?
A state wants an energy source that will not run out. Which choice is best?
A city got 30 percent of its electricity from renewable sources in 2015 and 55 percent in 2025. By how many percent did its renewable share increase?
Which is a drawback of solar power?
ch: It makes less electricity at night and on cloudy days.
It runs out after a few years.

quiz.q: A family's car used 12 gallons of gasoline a week. After they started biking to school, it used 9 gallons a week. How many gallons do they save in 4 weeks?
A student says, "Wind is better than coal in every way." Give one advantage and one disadvantage of wind compared with coal.
quiz.ans: Advantage: wind is renewable and does not make smoke or air pollution when it makes electricity. Disadvantage: wind does not blow all the time, so turbines do not always make electricity, and they need a lot of space.

lessons.name: How does using energy affect the environment?

practice.q: Burning fossil fuels in cars and power plants can
practice.h: Think about the exhaust from a car.

practice.q: Coal is often dug out of large mines. Which is an effect on the environment?
practice.h: What happens to the land when a large mine is dug?

practice.q: A dam on a river makes electricity but blocks salmon from swimming upstream. How could engineers reduce this problem?
ch: build a fish ladder that lets salmon pass the dam
practice.h: The fish need a path around the dam.

practice.q: A family switched 10 old light bulbs to LED bulbs. Each LED saves 50 units of electricity a year. How many units does the family save each year?
practice.h: Multiply the number of bulbs by the savings per bulb.

practice.q: Which choice reduces the amount of fuel people use?
ch: walking or biking for short trips
running the heater with windows open
practice.h: Which choice uses no fuel?

practice.q: Describe one way your class could use less energy at school and explain how it helps the environment.
practice.ans: Sample: Turn off computers and lights when we leave the room. Using less electricity means power plants burn less fuel, which means less air pollution.

quiz.q: Which energy resource releases the most air pollution when used?
Wind turbines make no smoke, but which effect on the environment can they have?
ch: Birds and bats can fly into the blades.

quiz.q: A school installs solar panels that make 3,000 units of electricity a month. The school uses 5,000 units a month. How many units must still come from other sources?
Which data would best help a town compare the environmental effects of two energy sources?
ch: how much air pollution each source makes and how much land each one uses
the color of each power plant
how many letters are in each name

quiz.q: An oil spill from a tanker reaches a beach. Which living things are most directly harmed?
ch: sea birds and ocean animals covered in oil
city pigeons far from the coast

quiz.q: A city bus carries 40 people and replaces 40 cars. If each car would have burned 2 gallons of gasoline on a trip and the bus burns 8 gallons, how many gallons are saved?

A town compared two energy plans. Plan A, a natural gas plant: works day and night, makes air pollution, costs less to build. Plan B, a solar farm with batteries: works in daytime and stores some energy for night, makes no air pollution when running, uses 200 acres of land. The town's main goal is to cut air pollution. Make a claim about which plan better meets the town's goal. Use evidence and explain your reasoning.
quiz.ans: Claim: Plan B, the solar farm with batteries, better meets the town's goal. Evidence: Plan B makes no air pollution when running, while Plan A makes air pollution. Plan B's batteries store energy so the town has some power at night. Reasoning: The town's main criterion is cutting air pollution. Sunlight is renewable and solar panels do not burn fuel, so Plan B meets the goal, even though it uses more land.
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

test.q: Which is a fossil fuel?
A resource that can be replaced naturally in a short time is
Which device changes sunlight directly into electricity?
Fossil fuels are nonrenewable because
ch: they take millions of years to form
they come from the Sun each day

test.q: Which energy resource depends on the weather?
Which statement about burning coal for electricity is true?
ch: It works day and night but pollutes the air.
It only works when the wind blows.

test.q: Which list shows only nonrenewable resources?
A hydroelectric dam uses which resource to make electricity?
Which action would reduce the amount of fossil fuel a family uses?
ch: leaving the car running while parked
using a gas heater with the door open

test.q: A school's electricity came 40 percent from solar and 25 percent from wind. The rest came from natural gas. What percent came from natural gas?
A home used 900 units of electricity in July and 620 units in October. How many fewer units did it use in October?
A family replaces 8 bulbs. Each new bulb saves 45 units of electricity a year. How many units do they save each year?
Which energy source has the problem that it can harm fish by blocking rivers?
A class graphed how much electricity a solar panel made each hour. The bars were tall around noon and zero at night. What does the graph show?
ch: Solar panels make the most electricity when the sun is strongest.
Solar panels work best at night.
Solar panels make the same amount all day.
Solar panels use coal at night.

test.q: A town has very steady winds, few sunny days and no rivers. Which renewable energy source is the best choice?
Why might a community use both solar and wind power instead of only one?
ch: When one is not available, like at night or on calm days, the other may still produce power.
Solar panels need wind to work.

test.q: A wind turbine makes about 25 units of electricity each hour on a windy day. How many units does it make in 8 hours?
Gasoline is made from which natural resource?
Which is an effect of mining for coal?
ch: More fish live in nearby streams.

test.q: Explain why getting more electricity from renewable resources is important for the future.
test.ans: Nonrenewable resources like coal and oil will run out and they pollute the air when burned. Renewable resources like sun and wind will not run out and make little or no pollution when used.

test.q: Describe one way people's use of energy affects the environment and one way to reduce that effect.
test.ans: Sample: Cars burn gasoline and pollute the air. People can walk, bike, carpool or use electric buses to burn less fuel.

test.q: A class measured car traffic and air quality near their school for two weeks. Week 1 (normal traffic, 600 cars a day): air quality index 85. Week 2 (a "walk to school" week, 250 cars a day): air quality index 55. A lower number means cleaner air. Make a claim about how car traffic affected air quality. Use evidence from the data and explain your reasoning.
test.ans: Claim: Fewer cars made the air near the school cleaner. Evidence: In Week 1 there were 600 cars a day and the index was 85. In Week 2 there were 250 cars a day and the index dropped to 55, which means cleaner air. Reasoning: Cars burn gasoline, a fossil fuel, and burning it releases pollution into the air. When fewer cars drove near the school, less fuel was burned, so less pollution was released.
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

units.name: Unit 4: Waves, Light and Information
units.el: Use a jump rope or slinky to act out amplitude (how high) and wavelength (peak to peak); label a large wave drawing together and give students a picture glossary for reflect, absorb, signal and code.

practice.q: The height of a wave from its resting position to its top is its
practice.h: Think "how tall."

practice.q: The distance from the top of one wave to the top of the next wave is the
practice.h: Measure from one peak to the next peak.

practice.q: A cork floats on a pond. Waves pass by. What does the cork mostly do?
ch: bobs up and down in about the same place
travels all the way across the pond with the waves
practice.h: Waves carry energy, not the water itself very far.

practice.q: Ocean waves with a very large amplitude crash on the beach. What can they do that small waves cannot?
ch: move larger rocks and wear away more sand
practice.h: A bigger amplitude means more energy.

practice.q: A wave model drawn on paper has peaks at 0 cm, 6 cm, 12 cm and 18 cm. What is its wavelength in centimeters?
practice.h: Find the distance between any two peaks next to each other.

practice.q: Draw or describe two waves: one with a large amplitude and short wavelength, and one with a small amplitude and long wavelength.
practice.ans: Wave 1 has tall peaks that are close together. Wave 2 has short, low peaks that are far apart.

quiz.q: Waves carry
A student shakes a rope harder and harder while keeping the same pace. Which part of the wave changes?
A student shakes a rope faster, making more waves each second. What happens to the wavelength?
A rope wave has peaks 40 cm apart. How far apart are the first peak and the fourth peak, in centimeters?
Which observation shows that waves can make objects move?
ch: A toy boat rocks up and down as ripples pass.
A rock sits still on the shore.
The sun shines on the water.
A fish sleeps on the bottom.

quiz.q: A class measured wave heights at the beach: 30 cm, 50 cm and 40 cm. What was the average wave height in centimeters? (Add and divide by 3.)
Explain why a surfer moves toward the beach on a wave but a floating leaf far from shore mostly bobs in place.
quiz.ans: A breaking wave near shore pushes the surfer forward. Out in deeper water, waves carry energy forward while the water and the leaf mostly move up and down in place.

lessons.name: What makes a sound loud or high?

practice.q: Sound is caused by
practice.h: Touch your throat while you hum.

practice.q: A drum is hit gently and then hard. The hard hit makes a louder sound because the sound wave has a
practice.h: Loudness is connected to the size of the vibration.

practice.q: A short guitar string makes a higher sound than a long string. In sound waves, a higher pitch has a
practice.h: Higher pitch means faster vibrations and waves closer together.

practice.q: Rice on a drum jumps more when the drum is hit harder. What does this show?
ch: Louder sound waves carry more energy.
practice.h: Compare how much the rice moved.

practice.q: A sound meter read 45 units for a whisper and 70 units for a shout. How many units louder was the shout?
practice.h: Subtract the whisper reading.

practice.q: Explain how you could make a rubber band make a higher sound and a louder sound.
practice.ans: Stretch it tighter or make it shorter for a higher pitch. Pluck it harder for a louder sound with a bigger amplitude.

quiz.q: Which part of a sound wave is related to how loud it is?
Two bottles have different amounts of water. Blowing across the bottle with less air space makes a higher sound. Which wave property is different?
ch: The higher sound has a shorter wavelength.
The higher sound has a longer wavelength.
The sounds have the same pitch.

quiz.q: Which change will make a xylophone note quieter?
A class measured the loudness of a bell at different distances. 1 meter: 80 units. 3 meters: 68 units. 5 meters: 59 units. How many units quieter was it at 5 meters than at 1 meter?
Using the same data (80, 68 and 59 units at 1, 3 and 5 meters), which pattern is shown?
ch: The farther away, the quieter the sound.
The farther away, the louder the sound.
The bell got louder over time.

quiz.q: A model of two sound waves shows Wave A with tall peaks far apart and Wave B with short peaks close together. Which description fits?
ch: Wave A is louder and lower; Wave B is quieter and higher.
Wave A is quieter and higher; Wave B is louder and lower.
Wave B is louder and lower.

quiz.q: Describe what happens to the energy of a sound wave as you move farther from the sound.
quiz.ans: The energy spreads out as the sound travels, so the amplitude gets smaller and the sound gets quieter the farther away you are.

practice.q: We see an object when light
ch: reflects off the object and enters our eyes
comes out of our eyes and hits the object
is absorbed completely by the object
practice.h: Light has to reach your eyes.

practice.q: In a completely dark room with no light at all, can you see a red ball?
ch: No, because no light reflects from it into your eyes.
Yes, if you look hard enough.
Only if the ball is big.
practice.h: What does seeing need?

practice.q: A mirror reflects light very well. Why can you see your face in it?
ch: Light reflects off your face, then off the mirror, into your eyes.
The mirror makes its own light.
Your eyes send light to the mirror.
The mirror absorbs all the light.
practice.h: Trace the light's path.

practice.q: A light beam travels 30 cm from a flashlight to a mirror and 45 cm from the mirror to a student's eye. How far does the light travel in all, in centimeters?
practice.h: Add both parts of the path.

practice.q: Which object reflects the least light?
practice.h: Dark colors absorb more light.

practice.q: Draw or describe a model that shows how you see a book on your desk while a lamp is on.
practice.ans: Arrows go from the lamp to the book, then from the book to my eye. Light from the lamp reflects off the book and enters my eye, and my brain makes sense of it.

quiz.q: Which part of the body takes in light so we can see?
A student shines a flashlight at a wall and a friend in another part of the room sees a bright spot. Which model is correct?
A periscope uses two mirrors to see over a wall. How does it work?
ch: Light reflects off one mirror and then the other into your eye.
Your eyes send beams to the mirrors.
The mirrors absorb all the light.

quiz.q: In a test, a white card reflected 85 units of light and a black card reflected 10 units. How many more units did the white card reflect?
Cats see well at night but still cannot see in total darkness. Why?
ch: Seeing needs some light to reflect off objects into the eyes.
Cats close their eyes at night.

quiz.q: A student holds a book in front of a mirror and sees the book in the mirror. What path did the light take?
ch: from a light source to the book, then to the mirror, then to the student's eyes
from the student's eyes to the mirror, then to the book
from the book straight into the light source
from the mirror into the book

quiz.q: A class tested how well materials reflect light. They aimed the same flashlight at each material from the same distance and used a light sensor. Mirror: 95 units. White paper: 70 units. Brown cardboard: 30 units. Black felt: 5 units. Make a claim about which material would be easiest to see in a dim room. Use evidence and explain your reasoning.
quiz.ans: Claim: The mirror, and then white paper, would be easiest to see in a dim room. Evidence: The mirror reflected 95 units and white paper 70 units, while black felt reflected only 5 units. Reasoning: We see objects when light reflects off them into our eyes. Materials that reflect more light send more light to our eyes, so they are easier to see when there is little light.
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

lessons.name: How can we send messages using patterns?

practice.q: A pattern of long and short signals used to send letters is a
practice.h: Morse code is one example.

practice.q: Two students send a message across the field by flashing a flashlight: one flash means "yes" and two flashes mean "no." What is being used to carry the information?
practice.h: What did they flash?

practice.q: Drums in some places were used long ago to send messages between villages. Why did this work?
ch: Patterns of drumbeats could travel as sound over a distance.
practice.h: How does sound get from one village to another?

practice.q: In a code, each letter uses 3 light flashes. How many flashes are needed for a 4-letter word?
practice.h: Multiply flashes per letter by the number of letters.

practice.q: A code uses 1 = on and 0 = off. Which pattern means on, off, on?
practice.h: Write 1 for on and 0 for off, in order.

practice.q: Design a simple code using claps to send the words "stop," "go" and "wait" to a teammate. Explain how your teammate would know which word you mean.
practice.ans: Sample: 1 clap = go, 2 claps = stop, 3 claps = wait. My teammate counts the claps, and each number stands for a different word.

quiz.q: Computers and phones send information as
ch: patterns of signals, such as 1s and 0s
magnets that fly through the air

quiz.q: Two teams sent the same 20-word message across a noisy gym. Team A used shouting: 9 words were wrong. Team B used a flashlight code: 2 words were wrong. Which conclusion is supported?
ch: In this test, the light code sent the message with fewer errors.

quiz.q: Using the same data (Team A had 9 wrong words and Team B had 2), how many more words did Team A get wrong?
Team B sent 20 words and got 2 wrong. How many words did Team B send correctly?
Which improvement would most likely reduce errors in a flashlight code?
ch: make every signal clearly long or short and repeat the message
send the message faster than the receiver can watch
turn the light off halfway through

quiz.q: Why do engineers compare several ways to send information?
ch: to find which way best meets criteria like speed, distance and accuracy
to use the most expensive way

quiz.q: A team's sound code worked across the classroom but not across the playground. Explain one likely reason and one way to improve the design.
quiz.ans: The sound got quieter as it traveled farther, so the receiver could not hear it clearly. They could use a louder sound, like a whistle, or switch to a light code that can be seen from far away.

test.q: The distance from one wave peak to the next is the
Sound is made by
We see an object because light
ch: reflects off the object into our eyes

test.q: A wave with a larger amplitude carries
ch: the same energy as any wave

test.q: A beach ball floats as ocean waves pass under it far from shore. What does the beach ball do?
ch: It moves up and down in about the same place.

test.q: A drum is hit harder. What happens to the sound?
ch: It gets louder because the amplitude is larger.
It gets higher because the wavelength is longer.

test.q: Which picture of a wave would show a higher-pitched sound?
Why can you not see your hand in a completely dark closet?
ch: No light reflects from your hand into your eyes.
Your hand disappears in the dark.

test.q: A student shines a flashlight at a mirror and the beam lights up a poster. Which describes the path of the light?
ch: the light goes straight through the mirror

test.q: A wave drawing has peaks at 0 cm, 8 cm, 16 cm and 24 cm. What is the wavelength in centimeters?
A team's code uses 4 beeps for each letter. How many beeps are needed for a 5-letter word?
A sound meter read 92 units next to a speaker and 58 units across the room. How many units quieter was it across the room?
In a code where 1 = flash on and 0 = flash off, what does 0110 mean?
Which material would reflect the most light?

Two students send messages across a field. Message A is a spoken sentence. Message B is a pattern of flag waves that each stand for a letter. On a windy, noisy day, which would most likely arrive with fewer errors, and why?
ch: Message B, because the flag pattern can be seen even when noise drowns out speech
Message A, because sound travels through wind easily
Both the same, because weather does not matter
Neither, because messages cannot travel across a field

test.q: A student makes two rope waves. Wave 1: amplitude 10 cm, wavelength 50 cm. Wave 2: amplitude 30 cm, wavelength 50 cm. Which is true?
Which sends information using patterns of electrical signals?
A class tested a flashlight code 3 times with a 15-word message. Errors: 3, 1 and 2. What was the average number of errors? (Add and divide by 3.)
Waves at a beach knock down a sandcastle. What does this show?
ch: Waves carry energy that can move objects.

test.q: Draw or describe a wave and label its amplitude and wavelength. Then describe how the wave would change if it carried more energy.
test.ans: A wave with peaks and troughs; amplitude is the height from the middle line to a peak, and wavelength is the distance from one peak to the next. With more energy, the amplitude would be larger, so the peaks would be taller.

test.q: Explain why a cat sitting in a dark room cannot be seen until someone turns on a lamp.
test.ans: We see objects only when light reflects off them into our eyes. Without the lamp, no light reflects from the cat, so we cannot see it.

test.q: A class tested two ways to send a 10-letter message 50 meters across the playground. Shouting: 4 letters wrong on a quiet day, 8 letters wrong on a windy day. Flashlight code (long and short flashes): 1 letter wrong on a quiet day, 1 letter wrong on a windy day. Make a claim about which method is the better design for sending messages across the playground. Use evidence from the data and explain your reasoning.
test.ans: Claim: The flashlight code is the better design. Evidence: It had only 1 wrong letter on both days, while shouting had 4 wrong on a quiet day and 8 on a windy day. Reasoning: The flashlight code uses patterns of light that are easy to tell apart and are not affected by wind noise. Shouted sound gets quieter over distance and is drowned out by wind, so more information was lost.
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

units.name: Unit 5: Structures, Senses and Survival
units.el: Use labeled photos and diagrams of plants and animals; teach structure (a part) and function (its job) with the frame "The ___ helps the ___ ___ by ___." Pair students to point to and name structures before writing.

lessons.name: How do plant structures help plants survive?

practice.q: Which plant structure takes in water and minerals from the soil?
practice.h: This part grows underground.

practice.q: Where does a plant make most of its food using sunlight?
practice.h: These parts are usually flat and green.

practice.q: A rose bush has sharp thorns on its stems. What is the function of the thorns?
ch: They protect the plant from animals that might eat it.
They help the plant drink water.
practice.h: Think about what an animal would feel if it bit the stem.

practice.q: Bright, sweet-smelling flowers help a plant
ch: attract pollinators so it can make seeds
practice.h: Bees and butterflies visit flowers.

practice.q: A class measured a sunflower stem. In week 1 it was 18 cm tall, and in week 4 it was 75 cm tall. How many centimeters did it grow?
practice.h: Subtract to find the change.

practice.q: Choose one plant structure and explain how it helps the plant survive, grow or reproduce.
practice.ans: Sample: The stem holds the plant up toward sunlight and carries water from the roots to the leaves.

quiz.q: Which plant structure helps make new plants?
A cactus has a thick, waxy stem and spines instead of broad leaves. How do these structures help it survive in the desert?
ch: They help it store water and lose less water.
They help it soak up rain from the air only.
They make it grow faster in the shade.

quiz.q: An apple tree makes fruit around its seeds. How does the fruit help the tree reproduce?
ch: Animals eat the fruit and spread the seeds to new places.
The fruit makes the tree taller.
The fruit keeps the roots warm.
The fruit makes food from sunlight.

quiz.q: A tomato plant made 14 tomatoes. Each tomato had about 60 seeds. About how many seeds were there in all?
A plant was left in a closet with no light for two weeks. Its leaves turned yellow. Which structure could not do its job?
ch: the leaves, which need light to make food
the roots, which need dark soil

quiz.q: Tall trees in a rain forest have wide, flared bases called buttress roots. What is the most likely function?
ch: to help hold the tall tree up in shallow soil
to catch rain on the leaves

quiz.q: Make an argument for how a pine tree's thick bark helps it survive.
quiz.ans: Thick bark is a hard outer covering that protects the inside of the tree from insects, from drying out and even from some fires, so the tree can keep growing.

lessons.name: How do animal body parts help them survive?

practice.q: A turtle's hard shell is an external structure that helps it
practice.h: Think about what a turtle does when it is in danger.

practice.q: An eagle has sharp, curved talons. What is their function?
ch: building a nest out of mud
practice.h: Talons are the eagle's claws.

practice.q: A duck has webbed feet. How do they help the duck?
ch: They push water to help it swim.
They keep it cool in the desert.
practice.h: Think about where ducks spend time.

practice.q: A porcupine is covered in sharp quills. Which statement is the best argument about this structure?
ch: The quills help the porcupine survive by keeping predators away.
The quills help the porcupine fly.
The quills help it see better.
The quills help it smell food.
practice.h: What would happen to an animal that tried to bite it?

practice.q: A hummingbird's beak is 2 cm long. A woodpecker's beak is 5 cm long. How many centimeters longer is the woodpecker's beak?
practice.h: Subtract the lengths.

practice.q: Describe an external structure of an animal that lives in a cold place and explain how it helps the animal survive.
practice.ans: Sample: A polar bear has thick fur and a layer of fat. The fur traps heat and the fat keeps the bear warm in icy water and snow.

quiz.q: Which is an external structure of a bird?
A giraffe's long neck helps it
Male peacocks have large, colorful tail feathers. How does this structure help with reproduction?
ch: It helps attract females so they can mate.
It helps them fly long distances.

quiz.q: Suppose scientists measured the fur of an Arctic fox in summer (3 cm thick) and winter (7 cm thick). How many centimeters thicker was the winter fur?
Using the same data (summer fur 3 cm thick and winter fur 7 cm thick), which is the best explanation for the change?
ch: Thicker fur helps the fox stay warm in the cold winter.
Thicker fur helps the fox stay cool.

quiz.q: A bird has a long, thin, pointed beak. Which food is it most likely adapted to eat?
Choose an animal and make an argument for how two of its external structures help it get food. Use evidence.
quiz.ans: Sample: A lion has sharp teeth and strong claws. The claws grab and hold prey, and the sharp teeth tear meat, so the lion can catch and eat other animals.

lessons.name: What structures inside the body help animals survive?

practice.q: Which internal organ pumps blood through the body?
practice.h: You can feel it beat in your chest.

practice.q: Which internal structures take in oxygen from the air?
practice.h: They fill up when you breathe in.

practice.q: A fish lives underwater. Which structure lets it get oxygen from water?
practice.h: Look at the slits on the sides of a fish's head.

practice.q: Many birds have hollow bones. How does this help them?
ch: Their light bones make flying easier.
Their bones make them heavier for diving.
practice.h: Think about what flying requires.

practice.q: A student counted her heartbeats for 15 seconds while resting: 21 beats. After jumping jacks, she counted 33 beats in 15 seconds. How many more beats did she count after exercise?
practice.h: Subtract the resting count.

practice.q: Explain how the skeleton and muscles work together to help an animal move.
practice.ans: The skeleton is a frame of bones that supports the body. Muscles attach to the bones and pull on them, which makes the body parts move.

quiz.q: The stomach's main function is to
A student's resting heart rate was 80 beats per minute. After running, it was 130 beats per minute. Why did it go up?
ch: The heart pumped faster to move more oxygen to the working muscles.
The lungs took over the heart's job.

quiz.q: Using the same data (80 beats per minute resting and 130 after running), how many more beats per minute was the heart rate after running?
A whale is a mammal that lives in the ocean. Why must it come to the surface?
ch: It needs to dry its gills.
It needs to see the Sun.

quiz.q: Which pair matches an internal structure with its function?
ch: brain - controls the body and processes information

quiz.q: An adult human skeleton has about 206 bones. A baby is born with about 270 bones, which grow together over time. About how many more bones does a baby have?
Make an argument for why the heart is important for an animal's survival.
quiz.ans: The heart pumps blood that carries oxygen and food to every part of the body. Without it, the body's cells would not get what they need, so the animal could not survive.

lessons.name: How do animals sense and respond to their surroundings?

practice.q: Which body part sends information from the senses to be processed?
practice.h: The brain is the body's control center.

practice.q: You touch a hot pan and quickly pull your hand away. In what order does this happen?
ch: skin senses heat -> nerves send a message -> muscles move the hand
muscles move -> skin senses heat -> brain forgets
brain moves the pan -> skin cools
eyes see the pan -> stomach responds
practice.h: Start with the sense organ.

practice.q: Owls hunt mice at night in dim light. Which senses most help them?
practice.h: Think about how to find a mouse in the dark.

practice.q: Bats send out high-pitched sounds and listen for the echoes. What does this help them do?
ch: find insects and avoid objects in the dark
practice.h: The echoes bounce off things.

practice.q: A student's reaction time was tested by catching a falling ruler. Trial 1: 18 cm. Trial 2: 14 cm. Trial 3: 13 cm. What was the average distance in centimeters? (Add the trials and divide by 3.)
practice.h: Add 18, 14 and 13, then divide by 3.

practice.q: Describe how a dog uses its senses to find a hidden treat. Name the sense, the sense organ and how the brain responds.
practice.ans: The dog smells the treat with its nose. Nerves send the smell information to the brain, which recognizes food and tells the dog's legs to move toward it.

quiz.q: Which organ processes information from the senses?
A rabbit hears a twig snap and freezes, then runs. Which statement explains this?
ch: Its ears sensed the sound, its brain processed it as danger and it responded by running.

quiz.q: A rattlesnake has pits on its face that sense heat. How does this help it hunt at night?
ch: It can sense the warm bodies of animals in the dark.

quiz.q: A class measured reaction time with a dropped ruler. Before practice, the average catch was 22 cm. After practice, it was 16 cm. How many centimeters better was the average after practice?
Some animals store memories of where they hid food. A squirrel buries acorns and later finds many of them. Which body part helps it remember?
A student models how we see a ball thrown at us and catch it. Which model is most complete?
ch: light from the ball enters the eyes, nerves carry signals to the brain, the brain sends signals to arm muscles
the ball sends sound to the ear and the ear catches it

quiz.q: Explain why animals that live in dark caves often have small eyes but a strong sense of touch or smell.
quiz.ans: In a dark cave there is little light, so eyes are less useful. Senses like touch and smell give the brain information about food and danger, which helps the animal survive.

test.q: Which plant structure holds the plant up and carries water to the leaves?
Which structure helps a fish get oxygen?
The brain's main job is to
ch: process information and control the body

test.q: A cactus has spines. Which is the best argument about their function?
ch: They protect the cactus from animals that want its water.
They help the cactus make seeds.
They help the cactus take in sunlight.

test.q: A polar bear's white fur helps it
ch: blend in with the snow while hunting

test.q: Which pair correctly matches an animal structure to its function?
A flower is brightly colored and has sweet nectar. Which statement explains how this helps the plant?
ch: It attracts animals that carry pollen so the plant can make seeds.
It keeps insects away from the plant.
It helps the plant take in water.
It makes the plant grow taller.

test.q: A student touches a cold ice cube and pulls her hand back. Which part sensed the cold?
Why does an animal's heart beat faster when it runs?
ch: to deliver more oxygen to its muscles

test.q: A class measured how far roots of two bean plants grew in one week: Plant A 12 cm and Plant B 19 cm. How many centimeters longer were Plant B's roots?
A student's breathing rate was 16 breaths per minute resting and 34 breaths per minute after running. How many more breaths per minute after running?
A ruler-drop test gave 20 cm, 17 cm and 14 cm. What was the average distance in centimeters? (Add and divide by 3.)
Bats find insects at night by
ch: sending out sounds and listening for echoes

test.q: A seed is covered by a hard coat. What is the function of the seed coat?
ch: to protect the young plant inside

test.q: A desert plant has long roots that reach deep under the ground. Which claim is best supported?
ch: The deep roots help the plant reach water far below the dry surface.
The deep roots help the plant catch insects.
The roots help the plant make seeds.
Deep roots make the plant shorter.

test.q: An animal has large ears, long legs and fur the color of sand. Which habitat is it most likely adapted to?
Which internal structure gives an animal's body shape and support?
A hummingbird's heart beats about 1,200 times a minute while flying and about 250 times a minute while resting. How many more beats per minute is that while flying?
A frog sees a fly, then flicks out its tongue to catch it. Which describes the order of events?
ch: eyes sense the fly -> brain processes it -> muscles move the tongue
tongue moves -> eyes see -> brain forgets
brain sees the fly -> eyes move the tongue
the fly signals the frog's stomach

test.q: Choose a plant. Describe one internal or external structure and argue how it helps the plant grow or reproduce.
test.ans: Sample: An oak tree's acorns are seeds with a hard shell. Squirrels carry and bury them, and some sprout into new oak trees, helping the oak reproduce.

test.q: Explain how a cat's senses, nerves and brain work together when it hears a mouse behind it.
test.ans: The cat's ears sense the sound. Nerves carry signals to the brain, which processes them as a possible meal and sends signals to the muscles so the cat turns and pounces.

test.q: Scientists compared two kinds of foxes. Arctic fox: ear length about 4 cm, thick white winter fur, lives where winter temperatures are often below -20°C. Fennec fox: ear length about 15 cm, thin sand-colored fur, lives in the Sahara desert where days can reach 45°C. Make a claim about how the foxes' external structures help them survive in their habitats. Use evidence and explain your reasoning.
test.ans: Claim: Each fox has external structures that help it survive in its own habitat. Evidence: The Arctic fox has short ears (about 4 cm) and thick white fur where it is below -20°C. The fennec fox has very large ears (about 15 cm) and thin sand-colored fur where it reaches 45°C. Reasoning: Small ears and thick fur hold in body heat, and white fur blends with snow. Large ears let heat escape and help the fennec fox hear prey, and sand-colored fur blends with the desert, so each fox's structures fit its environment.
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

units.name: Unit 6: Earth's Changing Surface and Natural Hazards
units.el: Build a stack of colored clay or paper layers to model rock layers; use photos of canyons, deltas and volcanoes, and pre-teach weathering (breaking down) and erosion (carrying away) with hand motions.

lessons.name: What can rock layers tell us about the past?

practice.q: In undisturbed rock layers, the oldest layer is usually
practice.h: Layers pile up over time, like a stack of newspapers.

practice.q: A layer of rock contains fossils of seashells and coral. What environment did that layer most likely form in?
practice.h: Where do seashells and coral live?

practice.q: A cliff has a bottom layer with fish fossils, a middle layer with fern fossils and a top layer with no fossils of water animals. Which story fits the layers?
ch: The area was underwater first, then later became land with plants.
The area was always a dry desert.
The area was land first and then the ocean.
The fossils were all buried at the same time.
practice.h: Read the layers from bottom (oldest) to top (newest).

practice.q: A layer of sediment builds up about 2 cm every 100 years. About how many centimeters would build up in 500 years?
practice.h: 500 years is five groups of 100 years.

practice.q: Which type of rock forms from layers of sand, mud and shells pressed together over a long time?
practice.h: "Sediment" means bits of sand, mud and shells.

practice.q: Explain how scientists can tell the order in which rock layers formed.
practice.ans: New layers are laid down on top of older layers, so in undisturbed rock the bottom layer formed first and the top layer formed last.

quiz.q: A fossil is found in a rock layer. What can it tell scientists?
ch: what lived in that area when the layer formed
what the weather will be next week
the color of the sky long ago

quiz.q: The walls of a canyon show many flat rock layers. A river flows at the bottom. Which explanation is best?
ch: The layers formed over a long time, and then the river slowly cut down through them.
The river made all the layers in one day.
The layers formed after the river dried up.

quiz.q: A layer with fossils of a tropical plant lies under a layer with fossils of animals that lived in cold places. What does this suggest?
ch: The climate changed from warm to cold over time.
The climate changed from cold to warm.
Plants and animals lived on top of each other.

quiz.q: A canyon wall is 360 meters tall. A river cut it about 1 meter deeper every 10,000 years. How many years would it take to cut 3 meters?
A rock layer has ripple marks like those on a sandy beach. What does this most likely show?
ch: The layer formed where moving water shaped the sand.
The layer formed in a volcano.
The layer is from outer space.

quiz.q: A model of rock layers has 5 layers. Each layer is 4 cm thick. How tall is the model in centimeters?
A fossil of a sea animal is found in a layer high up on a mountain. Use evidence to explain how this could happen.
quiz.ans: The fossil shows the layer formed under the sea. Over a very long time, forces inside Earth pushed the rock layers up to form the mountain.

lessons.name: How do water, wind, ice and plants change the land?

practice.q: The breaking of rock into smaller pieces is called
practice.h: "Weather" is in the word, but it means breaking down.

practice.q: The moving of rock and soil from one place to another is called
practice.h: This step carries pieces away.

practice.q: A class poured water over a sand hill model. With a small cup, little sand moved. With a big pitcher poured faster, a deep channel formed. What does this show?
ch: Faster, larger amounts of water cause more erosion.
Small cups cause the most erosion.
practice.h: Compare the amount and speed of the water.

practice.q: A tree's roots grow into a crack in a rock and make the crack wider. This is an example of
practice.h: The roots are breaking the rock.

practice.q: A riverbank wore away 15 cm in one year and 23 cm the next year after a big flood. How many centimeters did it wear away in both years?
practice.h: Add the two years.

practice.q: Water seeps into a crack in a rock and freezes. Explain how this can break the rock.
practice.ans: Water expands when it freezes into ice. The ice pushes on the sides of the crack and makes it bigger, and after many freezes and thaws the rock breaks apart.

quiz.q: Which can cause erosion?

A class tested how slope affects erosion. They poured 500 mL of water down a sand tray at three tilts. Low tilt: 20 g of sand moved. Medium tilt: 55 g moved. High tilt: 90 g moved. What pattern does the data show?
Using the same data (low tilt 20 g, medium tilt 55 g, high tilt 90 g), how many more grams of sand moved at high tilt than at low tilt?
A glacier slowly moves down a valley. What does it do to the land?
ch: scrapes and carves the valley wider and deeper

quiz.q: Planting grass on a hillside can reduce erosion because
ch: roots hold the soil in place

quiz.q: Sand dunes in a desert slowly move and change shape. What is the main cause?

Two hills were watered with the same amount of water in a model. Hill A, bare soil: 85 g of soil washed away. Hill B, covered with grass sod: 10 g washed away. Make a claim about how plants affect erosion. Use evidence and explain your reasoning.
quiz.ans: Claim: Plants reduce erosion. Evidence: The bare hill lost 85 g of soil, but the grass-covered hill lost only 10 g with the same amount of water. Reasoning: Plant roots hold soil particles together and leaves slow down falling water, so less soil is carried away when plants cover the ground.
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

lessons.name: Why are earthquakes and volcanoes found where they are?

practice.q: A map of earthquakes around the world shows that most earthquakes
ch: happen in long bands, often near the edges of continents and oceans
practice.h: Look for lines and patterns on the map.

practice.q: The "Ring of Fire" is a band of volcanoes and earthquakes around which ocean?
practice.h: California is on the edge of this ocean.

practice.q: A map shows that many tall mountain ranges, volcanoes and earthquakes are found in the same areas. What does this pattern suggest?
ch: The same forces inside Earth cause all three.
practice.h: Why would they be found together?

practice.q: A list shows 48 earthquakes in one month in California and 9 in Nevada. How many more were in California?
practice.h: Subtract the smaller number.

practice.q: Which California landform is a volcano?
practice.h: It is a tall, cone-shaped mountain in northern California.

practice.q: Describe what a map of volcanoes and earthquakes tells us about where they happen.
practice.ans: They are not spread out evenly. Most happen in bands along the edges of the giant plates of Earth's surface, such as around the Pacific Ocean.

quiz.q: Maps help scientists find
ch: patterns in where Earth's features and events occur

quiz.q: A map shows a deep ocean trench beside a chain of volcanoes. What is the best explanation?
ch: They formed where large plates of Earth's surface meet and move.
They formed in the middle of plates where nothing moves.

quiz.q: Why does California have many earthquakes?
ch: It sits along the boundary between two moving plates, such as along the San Andreas Fault.
It is in the middle of a plate.
It is near the North Pole.

quiz.q: In one year, a seismograph recorded 125 small earthquakes and 8 larger ones near a fault. How many earthquakes were recorded in all?
Most of the world's tallest mountains are found
ch: in long chains, often near plate edges
in perfect circles in the middle of oceans

quiz.q: A student marks the locations of 50 volcanoes on a world map. Most marks form a ring around the Pacific Ocean. What is the best prediction for a new volcano found next year?
ch: It will most likely be near the edge of the Pacific Ocean.
It will most likely be in the middle of a continent far from any plate edge.
It will be at the North Pole.
It will be in a lake.

quiz.q: Explain how a map of earthquakes could help a city decide where to build a new hospital.
quiz.ans: The map shows where earthquakes happen most often. The city could build in a place with fewer earthquakes or plan to build the hospital extra strong if it must be near a fault.

lessons.name: How can we reduce damage from natural hazards?

practice.q: Which is a natural hazard caused by Earth processes?
ch: a power outage from a broken cable
practice.h: It happens because of forces inside Earth.

practice.q: Which design helps a building stay standing during an earthquake?
ch: a flexible frame and pads under the base that let the ground move beneath it
walls that are not attached to the foundation
practice.h: Buildings that can sway a little are less likely to break.

practice.q: A community near the ocean worries about tsunamis after earthquakes. Which solution helps most?
ch: warning sirens and marked routes to higher ground
building homes closer to the beach
practice.h: What helps people get out of danger quickly?

practice.q: A model building on a shake table stayed standing for 8 seconds. After adding cross braces, it stayed standing for 25 seconds. How many seconds longer did it last?
practice.h: Subtract the times.

practice.q: Why do scientists place instruments around active volcanoes?
ch: to detect warning signs and alert people before an eruption
practice.h: Watching for changes helps people prepare.

practice.q: Name two solutions that reduce damage from landslides and explain one of them.
practice.ans: Building retaining walls and planting trees on slopes. A retaining wall holds back soil and rocks so they do not slide onto roads or homes.

quiz.q: Bolting a house to its foundation helps protect it from

A class tested three model buildings on a shake table. Model A (no braces): fell at 6 seconds. Model B (cross braces): fell at 20 seconds. Model C (cross braces and rubber pads under the base): still standing at 40 seconds when the test ended. Which design best reduces earthquake damage?
Using the same data (Model A fell at 6 seconds and Model B fell at 20 seconds), how many seconds longer did Model B last than Model A?
Model C costs twice as much as Model B. A town has a small budget but must protect a hospital. Which is the best reasoning?
ch: Choose Model C for the hospital because protecting people there is most important.
Choose Model A because it is cheapest.
Choose by the color of the model.

quiz.q: Which pair compares two solutions for reducing flood damage from heavy rains after a wildfire?
ch: planting fast-growing plants on burned slopes vs. building barriers to catch mud and rocks
painting houses vs. planting flowers indoors
turning off lights vs. closing windows
buying new cars vs. moving furniture

quiz.q: Each emergency kit costs $25. A school buys kits for 12 classrooms. How many dollars does it spend?

units.name: Unit 1: Cells - The Building Blocks of Life

They can all move from place to place
They all have leaves or roots
They are all large enough to see
practice.h: Think about the smallest unit that every living thing is built from.

ch: The tiny things are single-celled living organisms
The tiny things are dust floating in water

The tiny things are rocks that move with currents

ch: Cork is made of atoms you can see
Cells are only found in animals

practice.ans: A rock is not made of cells. Living things are made of one or more cells that use energy, grow and reproduce. Minerals piling up on a rock is not cell growth.

The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.
