test.q: Describe two ways the missions changed the land of California.
test.ans: Missions brought cattle, sheep, wheat and grapes, built adobe churches and irrigation ditches, and replaced wild plants Indians used with grazing land and fields.

test.q: Read the sources. Source A: Father Junipero Serra wrote in his letters that he hoped to bring Christianity to the native people of California. Source B: A chart of mission records shows that many more neophytes died than were born at most missions. Source C: The Tongva healer Toypurina said at her trial in 1785 that she joined the revolt because the missionaries were living on her people's land. Make a claim about how the mission system affected California Indians, and consider more than one point of view. Use evidence and reasoning.
test.ans: Claim: Although missionaries believed they were helping, the mission system caused great harm to California Indians. Evidence: Source A shows Serra's goal was to spread Christianity, his point of view; Source B shows deaths outnumbered births at the missions; Source C shows Toypurina resisted because missionaries took her people's land. Reasoning: The missionaries' religious goals did not match the experience of many Indians, who lost land and lives. Because deaths outnumbered births and leaders like Toypurina fought back, the evidence shows the missions were harmful to California Indians.
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

units.name: Unit 4: Mexican California, the Ranchos and the Mexican-American War (4.2, 4.3)
units.el: Pre-teach independence, secularization, land grant, rancho, Californio, vaquero, hide, tallow, revolt and treaty with picture cards. Use a two-column chart (before 1821 / after 1821) to compare Spanish and Mexican California.

practice.q: Mexico won its independence from Spain in
practice.h: The war for independence began in 1810 and ended eleven years later.

practice.q: After Mexico won independence, Alta California became
practice.h: Think about which country now ruled the land that Spain had claimed.

practice.q: Secularization of the missions meant
ch: mission lands were taken from the church and given to the government to divide
the missions were moved to Spain
practice.h: "Secular" means not religious.

practice.q: Mexico's law said much of the mission land should go to the California Indians who worked it. What actually happened to most of it?
ch: It was given as land grants to Californios and other settlers.
All of it went to the Indians.

practice.q: Mexico began secularizing the missions in 1834. How many years after the founding of the first mission in 1769 was that?
practice.h: Subtract 1769 from 1834.

practice.q: Explain one way life changed in Alta California after Mexico won independence.
practice.ans: Mexico ended the mission system, divided mission land into ranchos, opened trade with foreign ships, and Californios gained more power.

quiz.q: The capital of Mexican Alta California for most of the period was
Spain had limited trade with foreign ships. Mexico allowed more trade. What was one result?
ch: Ships from the United States and Britain came to buy hides and tallow.
California could only trade with Spain.

quiz.q: After secularization, many former neophytes
ch: had to find work on ranchos or in pueblos, often for little or no pay

quiz.q: The Mexican War for Independence changed the map of North America. Which land became part of Mexico in 1821?
ch: Alta California, Texas and the Southwest

quiz.q: Mexico ruled California from 1821 until the United States took control in 1846-1848. Using 1848, how many years was that?
A Californio landowner and a former mission neophyte both lived through secularization. How might their views differ?
ch: The landowner gained land and was pleased; the neophyte often lost a home and land that was promised.

quiz.q: Why did secularization fail to give most mission lands to California Indians?
quiz.ans: Officials and settlers took the land, Indians had little power or protection, and land grants went mostly to Californios and newcomers.

practice.q: A rancho was
ch: a large land grant used mainly for raising cattle
practice.h: Think of huge open grasslands and herds.

practice.q: Cattle hides were called "California bank notes" because
practice.h: How did people pay for goods when there was little money?

practice.q: Most of the work on the ranchos was done by
ch: California Indian workers, including many skilled vaqueros
practice.h: Many of these workers had learned ranching at the missions.

practice.q: Tallow is
ch: fat from cattle used to make candles and soap
practice.h: Think about what ranchers could make from every part of a cow.

practice.q: Ships from Boston sailed to California to buy hides. What did the ships bring to trade?
practice.h: California had few factories. What goods would people there want?

practice.q: Describe a day on a rancho for the ranchero's family and for an Indian vaquero.
practice.ans: The ranchero family managed the land, hosted guests and oversaw the herds; the vaquero rode long hours herding, roping and branding cattle, often for food and shelter instead of wages.

quiz.q: Californios were
At a yearly rodeo, vaqueros
ch: rounded up and branded the cattle

quiz.q: Richard Henry Dana worked on a ship collecting hides along the California coast in 1835 and wrote a book about it. Why is his book useful today?
ch: It is a primary source describing the hide trade and coastal life.
It was written by a Californio.

quiz.q: Juana Briones was a businesswoman who owned land and ran a dairy in Mexican California. What does her life show?
ch: Some women owned property and businesses in Mexican California.
Women could not own land at all.

quiz.q: A rancho sold 500 hides to a ship. Each hide was worth about $2 in trade. What was the total value of the hides?
A ranchero had 4,000 cattle. Vaqueros branded 1,250 new calves at the rodeo. How many cattle were there after the rodeo?
Explain how the hide and tallow trade connected Mexican California to the rest of the world.
quiz.ans: Californios traded hides and tallow to ships from Boston and other places for manufactured goods. Hides were made into shoes and goods in New England factories, so California became part of a world trade network.

practice.q: In 1812, Russian fur traders built a settlement on the northern California coast called
practice.h: Its name comes from an old word for Russia.

practice.q: John Sutter, a Swiss immigrant, built a fort and trading post in the Sacramento Valley in
practice.h: It was a stopping place for overland travelers in the 1840s.

practice.q: In 1841, the Bidwell-Bartleson Party became one of the first groups of American settlers to
ch: travel by wagon over land to California
practice.h: They crossed the Great Basin and the Sierra Nevada.

practice.q: James Beckwourth, an African American mountain man and trail guide, is remembered for
ch: finding a pass through the Sierra Nevada that wagons could use
practice.h: Mountain men knew routes through rough country.

practice.q: The Donner Party was trapped by snow in the Sierra Nevada in the winter of 1846-1847. What lesson did it teach other travelers?
ch: Leave early enough to cross the mountains before winter.
practice.h: Think about what the weather is like in the mountains in winter.

practice.q: Compare two ways newcomers traveled to California in the 1840s. Give one danger of each.
practice.ans: By wagon over land: deserts, mountains, snow and running out of food. By ship around South America: storms, disease and a very long trip of many months.

quiz.q: Many overland travelers in the 1840s stopped at which settlement before going on?
Why did American settlers come to Mexican California in the 1840s?
ch: to find good farmland and new opportunities

quiz.q: John C. Fremont led U.S. Army mapping expeditions to the West in the 1840s. What did his maps and reports do?
ch: They encouraged more Americans to move west to California.
They kept people away from California.

quiz.q: How did California Indians and Californios view the growing number of American settlers?
ch: Many were worried the newcomers would take land and power.
They asked them to build missions.

quiz.q: A wagon train traveled about 2,000 miles and took about 5 months. About how many miles did it travel each month?
Fort Ross was founded in 1812 and sold to John Sutter in 1841. How many years did the Russians stay?
Choose one person: John Sutter, James Beckwourth or John Bidwell. Explain how that person helped bring newcomers to California.
quiz.ans: Beckwourth found a lower pass through the Sierra and guided wagon trains; Sutter's Fort gave travelers supplies and work; Bidwell led one of the first overland wagon groups and later farmed and led in California.

lessons.name: The Bear Flag Revolt and the Mexican-American War

practice.q: In June 1846, American settlers in Sonoma declared California independent and raised a flag with a grizzly bear. This was the
practice.h: The flag gives the event its name.

practice.q: During the revolt, settlers took Mariano Guadalupe Vallejo prisoner. Who was he?
ch: a leading Californio and Mexican army general
practice.h: He lived in Sonoma and was one of the most powerful Californios.

practice.q: The Bear Flag Republic began June 14, 1846, and ended when the U.S. flag was raised in Sonoma on July 9, 1846. How many days did it last?
practice.h: Count the days left in June after the 14th, then add the days in July.

practice.q: The Mexican-American War was fought between the United States and Mexico from
practice.h: It began the same year as the Bear Flag Revolt and ended with a treaty in 1848.

practice.q: At the Battle of San Pasqual in December 1846, Californio soldiers on horseback with lances
ch: defeated U.S. troops led by Stephen Kearny
practice.h: The Californios were skilled riders who knew the land.

practice.q: Why did many Californios oppose the Bear Flag Revolt?
practice.ans: It was an attack on their country by newcomers who took their leaders prisoner and threatened their land and way of life.

quiz.q: The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, signed in 1848, ended the Mexican-American War and
ch: gave California and much of the Southwest to the United States

quiz.q: The treaty promised that Mexicans who stayed in California could keep their property. What happened to many Californios later?
ch: They lost land in costly court cases and to squatters.

quiz.q: Why is the bear still on California's state flag today?
ch: The Bear Flag Revolt is remembered as part of California's path to statehood.
Bears are the state's only animal.

quiz.q: A Californio wrote that the Bear Flaggers were thieves who stole horses. An American settler called them heroes. What explains the difference?
ch: They had different points of view about who had a right to the land.
One of them was not in California.

quiz.q: The war began in 1846, and the treaty was signed in 1848. In what year was the 150th anniversary of the treaty?
Which is the best order of events?
ch: Mexican independence, Bear Flag Revolt, Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo
Bear Flag Revolt, Mexican independence, Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo
Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, Bear Flag Revolt, Mexican independence
Mexican independence, Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, Bear Flag Revolt

quiz.q: Explain how the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo changed the lives of the people living in California.
quiz.ans: California became part of the United States; Californios and California Indians came under U.S. laws; many Californios later lost land, and California Indians lost even more land and rights.

test.q: Mexico won independence from Spain in
Large land grants used to raise cattle in Mexican California were
Spanish-speaking residents of Mexican California were called
Which products were the main exports of Mexican California?
What happened during the secularization of the missions?
ch: Church control ended and mission lands were divided, mostly into ranchos.

test.q: Who did most of the hard work on the ranchos?
Why did Russia build Fort Ross?
ch: to hunt sea otters for fur and grow food for Russian Alaska

test.q: Why did Sutter's Fort become important to overland travelers?
ch: It offered supplies, work and shelter at the end of the trail.
It was the capital of Mexico.

test.q: Which group of travelers was trapped by snow in the Sierra Nevada in 1846-1847?
What was the Bear Flag Revolt?
ch: a 1846 uprising by American settlers against Mexican rule in California
a battle between Spain and Russia
a Chumash uprising at the missions

test.q: Which treaty gave California to the United States?
Who was the last governor of Mexican California?
Mexico ruled California from 1821 to 1846. How many years is that?
A wagon trip of 2,000 miles took 4 months. About how many miles per month did the travelers go?
A ranchero traded 300 hides for cloth and 150 hides for tools. Each hide was worth $2. What was the total value of the hides he traded?
A Californio family received a land grant in 1840. In 1855, a U.S. court asked them to prove they owned it. Why was this a problem for many Californios?
ch: Old Mexican records and boundaries were often unclear, and court cases were costly and long.
U.S. courts gave everyone free land.

test.q: Which statement compares the mission and rancho periods correctly?
ch: Both relied on California Indian labor, but ranchos were owned by private families instead of the church.
Both were run by the U.S. government.

test.q: An American settler's diary calls California "a land waiting for us." A Californio's letter calls the settlers "intruders." What is the best conclusion?
ch: People saw the same events differently because they had different interests in the land.
The diary is true and the letter is false.
The letter is true and the diary is false.

test.q: How did the hide trade affect California Indians?
ch: Many worked long hours as vaqueros and laborers on ranchos with little pay.
They became owners of the trading ships.
They were not involved in it.

test.q: Describe how the end of Mexican rule changed life for Californios.
test.ans: They became part of the United States, faced new laws in English, and many lost their land through court cases, squatters and debts.

test.q: Explain why the hide and tallow trade was important to the rancho economy.
test.ans: Hides and tallow were traded to foreign ships for goods Californios could not make, so cattle were the main source of wealth.

test.q: Read the sources. Source A: The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo (1848) promised that Mexicans in the new U.S. lands would have their property "inviolably respected." Source B: A chart shows that in 1846, most land around Los Angeles was owned by Californio families, but by 1880, most was owned by newcomers. Source C: A historian explains that the Land Act of 1851 required landowners to prove their titles in U.S. courts, which often took years and cost a great deal. Make a claim about whether the United States kept its promise to Californios. Use evidence and reasoning.
test.ans: Claim: The United States did not fully keep its promise to protect Californio property. Evidence: Source A shows the treaty promised to respect Mexican property; Source B shows most land around Los Angeles passed from Californios to newcomers between 1846 and 1880; Source C shows the Land Act forced long, expensive court cases. Reasoning: Even though the treaty promised protection, new laws made it hard and costly for Californios to keep their land, so many lost it. The result went against the treaty's promise.
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

units.name: Unit 5: The Gold Rush and Statehood (4.3)
units.el: Show a picture timeline (1848 gold found, 1849 forty-niners, 1849 convention, 1850 statehood). Pre-teach claim, prospector, merchant, boomtown, tax, discrimination, delegate and constitution, and give the frame "The Gold Rush changed ___ because ___."

practice.q: Gold was found at Sutter's Mill on the American River in January of
practice.h: The people who rushed in the next year were named for that next year.

practice.q: Who found the first flakes of gold at Sutter's Mill?
practice.h: He was building a sawmill for Sutter.

practice.q: Henry Bigler, a worker at the mill, wrote in his diary on January 24, 1848: "This day some kind of mettle was found in the tail race that looks like goald." Why is this diary a primary source?
ch: It was written by a person who was there when it happened.
practice.h: Think about who wrote it and when.

practice.q: People who came to California for gold in 1849 were called
A ship from New York sailed about 13,000 miles around South America to San Francisco. Another route through Panama was about 5,000 miles. How many miles shorter was the Panama route?
practice.h: Subtract the shorter route from the longer one.

practice.q: Name two routes the forty-niners used to reach California and one hardship of each.
practice.ans: Overland by wagon: deserts, mountains, disease and lack of water. Around South America by ship: storms, seasickness and a trip of five to eight months. Across Panama: jungle diseases like malaria.

quiz.q: Gold was discovered in the foothills of which mountain range?
Sutter wanted to keep the discovery secret. Why?
ch: He feared workers would leave and people would take over his land.
He wanted to give the gold to Mexico.
He wanted to build a mission.

quiz.q: How did news of the gold spread around the world?
ch: by newspapers, letters and ships' sailors

quiz.q: Why did people come from places like Chile, Mexico, China, Australia and France?
ch: They hoped to get rich and send money home.

quiz.q: About 1,000 people lived in San Francisco in early 1848. By the end of 1849, about 25,000 people lived there. How many more people is that?
Gold was found in January 1848. The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo was signed in February 1848. What does this timing tell you?
ch: Mexico gave up California just as its gold was being discovered.
Mexico knew about the gold and wanted to sell it.
The treaty caused the gold to form.
The gold was found after statehood.

quiz.q: Why do you think news of the gold made so many people leave their homes and families?
quiz.ans: Gold seemed easy to find, so people hoped to get rich quickly, pay debts or help their families. Many were poor or had few chances at home.

practice.q: A shallow metal pan used to wash gravel and find gold is a
practice.h: The name of the tool is in the answer.

practice.q: Miners from Sonora, Mexico, and from Chile were often skilled because
ch: many had mined gold and silver at home
practice.h: Think about the mining history of Mexico and South America.

practice.q: In 1850, California passed a Foreign Miners' Tax of $20 a month. Who did it hurt most?
ch: miners from Mexico, Chile and China
miners born in the United States
practice.h: The tax was only for miners who were not U.S. citizens.

practice.q: A miner paid the $20 Foreign Miners' Tax every month for 6 months. How much did he pay?
practice.h: Multiply the monthly tax by the number of months.

practice.q: Hydraulic mining sprayed water through big hoses to wash away hillsides. What was one effect?
ch: Mud and gravel filled rivers and flooded farms downstream.

practice.q: Describe a day in the life of a gold miner in 1850. Include work, food and living conditions.
practice.ans: Miners worked from dawn digging and washing gravel in cold streams, lived in tents or cabins, ate beans, bread and salted meat bought at high prices, and often got sick.

quiz.q: A long wooden trough that used running water to separate gold from dirt was a
How did the Gold Rush affect California Indians?
ch: Miners took their land, polluted rivers, and many were killed or forced off their homelands.

quiz.q: In 1852, Norman Asing, a Chinese merchant in San Francisco, wrote a letter to Governor John Bigler, who wanted to stop Chinese immigration. Asing wrote: "We are not the degraded race you would make us." What was Asing's purpose?
ch: to defend the Chinese community against unfair treatment
to ask Chinese miners to leave

quiz.q: Louise Clappe wrote letters from a mining camp in 1851 and 1852 under the name "Dame Shirley." Why are her letters valuable?
ch: They describe daily life in a mining camp from a woman's point of view.
They describe life in Mexico City.

quiz.q: Why did most miners not get rich?
ch: The easy gold was found quickly, and prices for food and tools were very high.
There was no gold at all.

quiz.q: A miner found $16 of gold one week. He spent $12 on food and supplies. How much did he have left?
Explain how the Foreign Miners' Tax shows that not everyone was treated fairly during the Gold Rush.
quiz.ans: The tax made foreign miners, especially Mexican, Chilean and Chinese miners, pay $20 a month when U.S. miners paid nothing. Many were forced out of the mines, which was unfair because they had the same right to work.

practice.q: A town that grows very quickly is a
practice.h: Think of a sudden loud "boom."

practice.q: Which group often made more money than the miners?
ch: merchants who sold supplies to miners
practice.h: Every miner needed food, tools and clothes.

practice.q: Levi Strauss came to San Francisco in 1853 and sold cloth and goods. He later became famous for
ch: sturdy work pants called blue jeans
practice.h: Miners needed clothes that would not tear while they worked.

practice.q: Biddy Mason was brought to California as an enslaved woman. In 1856 she
ch: went to court in Los Angeles and won freedom for herself and her family
practice.h: California's constitution did not allow slavery.

practice.q: When the gold ran out, many mining towns were abandoned and became
practice.h: Think about what a town becomes when everyone leaves.

practice.q: Explain why Sacramento and San Francisco grew so fast during the Gold Rush.
practice.ans: San Francisco had a harbor where ships brought people and supplies; Sacramento was on rivers near the gold fields. Both became trade and supply centers for miners.

quiz.q: Which city became the main port for people arriving by sea during the Gold Rush?
Biddy Mason later bought land, worked as a nurse and helped start a church. What does her story show?
ch: African American women helped build early California communities.
No one could own land in Los Angeles.

quiz.q: A miner in 1849 could pay $1 for one egg. Why were prices so high?
ch: Many people wanted goods, but there were few goods to buy.

quiz.q: Many Chinese immigrants opened businesses in San Francisco, such as restaurants, laundries and stores. The neighborhood where many lived became
A store sold shovels for $10 each. It sold 45 shovels in one week. How much money did it take in?
A table shows California's population was about 93,000 in 1850 and about 380,000 in 1860. How many more people lived in California in 1860?
Choose a person who succeeded in Gold Rush California without mining, such as Levi Strauss or Biddy Mason. Explain how that person contributed.
quiz.ans: Levi Strauss sold goods and made strong work pants that miners needed; Biddy Mason won her freedom, bought land, nursed the sick and helped her community.

practice.q: California became a state on September 9 of
practice.h: It was two years after gold was found.

practice.q: In 1849, delegates met at Colton Hall in Monterey to write
practice.h: A state needs a plan of government before it can join the union.

practice.q: California's 1849 constitution was printed in two languages. Which ones?
practice.h: Think about who lived in California at the time.

practice.q: The 1849 constitution said: "Neither slavery, nor involuntary servitude, unless for the punishment of crimes, shall ever be tolerated in this State." What did this mean?
ch: California would be a free state.

practice.q: California became the 31st state in 1850. How many years later did it celebrate 150 years of statehood? Give the year.
practice.h: Add 150 to the year of statehood.

practice.q: Explain why California became a state so quickly after the Gold Rush began.
practice.ans: The Gold Rush brought so many people that California needed a government, courts and laws to keep order and protect property, so leaders wrote a constitution and asked to join the union.

quiz.q: The first state capital of California in 1850 was
Some delegates at the 1849 convention were Californios, such as Mariano Vallejo. Why was this important?
ch: Californios had a voice in the new government.
Californios wrote the Treaty of Paris.
They wanted California to stay in Spain.

quiz.q: California's entry as a free state upset the balance between free and slave states in Congress. The deal that let it join was the
How was California's new state government different from government under Mexico?
ch: It had an elected legislature and governor under a written state constitution within the United States.
It was ruled by a Spanish king.
It was run by mission priests.

quiz.q: The 1849 constitution allowed only white male citizens to vote. Which group could NOT vote?
ch: Californio men who chose to become U.S. citizens

quiz.q: The capital moved to Sacramento in 1854. How many years after statehood was that?
A newspaper in 1850 celebrated statehood. A California Indian elder at the same time might have felt differently. Why?
ch: Statehood brought new laws that took away Indian land and rights.
Statehood had nothing to do with Indians.

quiz.q: Explain one way the 1849 constitution protected freedom and one way it did not treat all Californians equally.
quiz.ans: It banned slavery, protecting freedom. But it let only white male citizens vote, leaving out women, California Indians, African Americans and Chinese immigrants.

test.q: Where was gold discovered in 1848?
ch: Sutter's Mill on the American River

test.q: In what year did California become a state?
People who came to California looking for gold in 1849 were called
Which group often became the richest from the Gold Rush?
The Foreign Miners' Tax mainly targeted
What happened to San Francisco during the Gold Rush?
ch: It grew from a small town into a busy city.
It became the capital of Mexico.

test.q: Which was an effect of hydraulic mining on the environment?
ch: Rivers filled with mud and gravel and farms flooded.

test.q: Which statement about the Gold Rush and California Indians is true?
ch: Their population fell sharply because of violence, disease and loss of land.
They were given gold claims by the state.

test.q: Biddy Mason is remembered because she
ch: won her freedom in court and became a leader in Los Angeles

test.q: California entered the United States as a
Which document set up California's state government?
Why did the Compromise of 1850 matter to California?
ch: It allowed California to join the union as a free state.

test.q: Gold was discovered in 1848 and California became a state in 1850. How many years apart are these events?
A miner paid $20 a month in Foreign Miners' Tax for 1 year. How much tax did he pay?
California had about 93,000 people in 1850. San Francisco had about 25,000 of them in 1849. Using these numbers, about how many Californians did NOT live in San Francisco?
A miner's letter says, "I have found only a little gold, and everything costs ten times what it did at home." What can you infer?
ch: Mining was hard, and high prices made it difficult to save money.

test.q: Which pair shows a cause and its effect?
ch: Gold is discovered - thousands of people move to California.
California becomes a state - gold is discovered.
The Gold Rush ends - San Francisco is founded.
The missions are built - the Gold Rush starts.

test.q: Norman Asing's 1852 letter to the governor and the Foreign Miners' Tax both show
ch: that Chinese and other immigrants faced discrimination and some spoke out against it
that all immigrants were treated equally
that the tax helped Chinese miners

test.q: Why did many mining towns become ghost towns?
ch: The gold ran out and people left.
The towns were flooded by the ocean.

test.q: Describe two ways the Gold Rush changed California's economy.
test.ans: Cities and businesses grew to serve miners, prices rose, new farms and ranches fed the population, banks and shipping grew, and California's trade with the world increased.

test.q: Explain why California's path to statehood was unusual.
test.ans: California never became an official territory first. Because of the Gold Rush population boom, it wrote a constitution in 1849 and became a state in 1850.

test.q: Read the sources. Source A: A chart shows California's non-Indian population grew from about 14,000 in 1848 to about 93,000 in 1850. Source B: A letter from a miner in 1850 complains there are "no courts, no sheriffs, and every man protects his own claim with a gun." Source C: The 1849 constitutional convention met in Monterey and set up a governor, a legislature and courts. Make a claim about why Californians wanted statehood in 1849 and 1850. Use evidence and reasoning.
test.ans: Claim: The Gold Rush brought so many people so fast that Californians needed a real government, so they asked for statehood. Evidence: Source A shows the population grew about six times in two years; Source B shows there were no courts or sheriffs to settle claims; Source C shows the convention created a governor, legislature and courts. Reasoning: A large, fast-growing population with no laws or courts leads to disorder and fights over claims. A state government could make and enforce laws, so Californians wrote a constitution and joined the union.
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

units.name: Unit 6: Railroads, Immigration and Growth (4.4)
units.el: Use a world map to show where immigrants came from, with arrows to California. Pre-teach immigrant, migrant, telegraph, transcontinental, exclusion and discrimination, and give the frame "___ came to California from ___ because ___."

practice.q: The Pony Express carried mail on horseback between St. Joseph, Missouri, and Sacramento starting in
practice.h: It began about ten years after statehood.

practice.q: The Pony Express ended in October 1861. What replaced it?
practice.h: This invention sent messages over wires in minutes.

practice.q: The Pony Express route was about 1,900 miles. Riders took about 10 days. About how many miles did the mail travel each day?
practice.h: Divide the miles by the number of days.

practice.q: Why did Californians want faster mail and travel to the East?
ch: California was far from the rest of the country, and news took weeks or months to arrive.
They wanted to stop all trade.
They wanted to move back to Mexico.

practice.q: Stagecoaches of the Overland Mail Company carried mail and passengers to California beginning in 1858. About how long did the trip take?
practice.h: Stagecoaches were faster than wagon trains but much slower than trains.

practice.q: Explain why the Pony Express lasted less than two years but is still remembered.
practice.ans: The telegraph made it unnecessary in 1861. It is remembered because it was fast for its time and showed how much Californians wanted to be connected to the nation.

quiz.q: The telegraph sent messages using
Which order is correct, from earliest to latest?
ch: Overland Mail stagecoaches, Pony Express, transcontinental telegraph

quiz.q: Pony Express riders changed to fresh horses at stations along the route. Why?

Source A (timeline): 10,000 BCE farming begins in the Fertile Crescent; 7000 BCE villages such as Catalhoyuk have thousands of people; 3500 BCE cities grow in Sumer. Make a claim about how farming led to the rise of civilization. Use evidence from both sources and explain your reasoning.
test.ans: Claim: Farming led to civilization because it produced a surplus that allowed cities, specialized jobs and government to develop. Evidence: Source A shows farming came first, then large villages, then cities. Source B shows cities with workshops for potters and metalworkers and tablets recording stored grain. Reasoning: Stored grain means farmers grew more food than they needed, which freed others to become craftspeople and priests, and records of the grain show an organized government managing the surplus.

Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

units.name: Unit 2: Mesopotamia (6.2)
units.el: Label a large map of the Tigris and Euphrates together, then use the frame "Because the rivers ___, the Sumerians ___." Pre-teach irrigation, city-state, ziggurat, scribe, cuneiform and code with pictures.

practice.q: The name Mesopotamia comes from Greek words meaning
practice.h: Look at where Mesopotamia sits on a map.

practice.q: Mesopotamia lay between which two rivers?
ch: the Huang He and the Yangtze
practice.h: Both rivers begin in the mountains of present-day Turkey.

practice.q: Southern Mesopotamia got very little rain. How did farmers there water their crops?
ch: They dug canals to carry river water to their fields
They melted snow from local mountains
They grew only crops that need no water
practice.h: Think of the word irrigation.

practice.q: The Tigris and Euphrates flooded at unpredictable times. How did Sumerians protect their fields?
ch: They built earthen walls called levees and stored water in basins
practice.h: Farmers needed to control both too little and too much water.

practice.q: On a map, 1 centimeter equals 100 kilometers. The Euphrates River flows about 28 centimeters on the map. About how many kilometers long is the river on this map?
practice.h: Multiply the map length by the scale.

practice.q: Explain one way the rivers helped the people of Mesopotamia and one way the rivers were a danger.
practice.ans: Help: the rivers gave water for irrigation and left rich silt for farming, and they were used for travel and trade. Danger: unpredictable floods could destroy crops, homes and canals.
practice.h: Think about both the gifts and the risks of a river.

quiz.q: The Fertile Crescent is a curved region of good farmland that stretches from the Persian Gulf to the
Mesopotamia had few trees and little stone. What building material did Sumerians use most?
ch: mud bricks dried in the sun

quiz.q: Because Mesopotamia lacked metals, timber and stone, Sumerians
ch: traded grain and cloth with other regions for these goods

quiz.q: Rich soil in Mesopotamia came from
ch: silt the rivers left behind after floods

quiz.q: Which job would be most important for keeping a Sumerian city fed?
ch: workers who kept the irrigation canals clean

quiz.q: A canal is 4,500 meters long. A crew of workers clears 150 meters of mud from it each day. How many days does it take to clear the whole canal?
A farmer in northern Mesopotamia, where more rain fell, and a farmer in the far south were compared. Which statement is most likely true?
ch: The southern farmer depended more on irrigation
The northern farmer depended more on irrigation
Both farmers lived in a rainforest

quiz.q: Explain how the need for irrigation helped lead to strong governments in Mesopotamia.
quiz.ans: Canals and levees were large projects that needed many workers and someone to plan, organize and settle disputes over water, so leaders and governments grew stronger.

practice.q: A city-state is
ch: a city and the farmland around it with its own government
a group of nations ruled by an emperor
a farming village with no leader
practice.h: Ur, Uruk and Lagash each had their own ruler.

practice.q: A ziggurat was a
ch: stepped temple tower at the center of a Sumerian city
practice.h: It rose in layers like a staircase.

practice.q: Sumerians practiced polytheism. This means they
practice.h: Poly means many; theism means belief in gods.

practice.q: Why did Sumerian city-states often fight one another?
ch: They competed for water, land and control of canals
They were all ruled by Egypt
practice.h: What resource was most precious in a dry land?

practice.q: A ziggurat had 3 levels. The bottom level was 60 meters wide, and each higher level was 15 meters narrower than the one below it. How wide was the top level?
practice.h: Subtract 15 for each level above the bottom.

practice.q: Describe the social classes of Sumer from top to bottom.
practice.ans: At the top were kings, priests and nobles; in the middle were merchants, artisans and farmers; at the bottom were enslaved people, often prisoners of war or people in debt.
practice.h: Think of who held power, who worked, and who was not free.

quiz.q: In early Sumer, who often held great power alongside the king?
Why did Sumerian cities build thick walls?
ch: to protect themselves from attacks by other city-states and raiders
to keep floods out of the desert
to show the border with China

quiz.q: Sumerians believed the gods controlled nature. How did this belief affect daily life?
ch: People made offerings at temples so the gods would send good harvests and protect the city

quiz.q: Which person would most likely be found at the bottom of Sumerian society?
Over time, many Sumerian city-states became ruled by kings because
ch: war leaders kept power after fighting ended and passed it to their sons
the people voted for a democracy

quiz.q: The city of Uruk may have had about 40,000 people. A smaller city-state had about 10,000 people. How many times larger was Uruk?
Which piece of evidence best shows that religion was at the center of Sumerian life?
ch: The largest building in each city was a ziggurat temple

quiz.q: Source A: In Sumerian cities, the ziggurat stood in the center, and temple storehouses held grain, tools and livestock. Source B: Clay tablets show temple workers giving out food rations to laborers and craftspeople. Make a claim about the role of temples in Sumerian city-states. Use evidence from both sources and explain your reasoning.
quiz.ans: Claim: Temples were centers of both religion and the economy. Evidence: Source A shows the ziggurat at the center of the city and temple storehouses holding grain, tools and animals. Source B shows temple workers paying food rations to workers. Reasoning: Because temples stored goods and paid workers, they controlled much of the city's wealth as well as its worship.

Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.

practice.q: The wedge-shaped writing system of Mesopotamia is called
practice.h: Cuneus is the Latin word for wedge.

practice.q: Sumerian scribes wrote by pressing a reed stylus into
practice.h: Mesopotamia had plenty of river mud.

send messages to Egypt by mail

practice.h: It is pulled through the ground by oxen.

practice.q: Sumerians used a number system based on 60, which we still use to measure time. How many minutes are in 3 hours?
practice.h: Each hour has 60 minutes.

practice.q: Why did becoming a scribe take many years of school in Sumer?
practice.ans: Cuneiform had hundreds of signs to memorize, so students practiced copying them for years.
practice.h: How many signs did a scribe need to learn?

quiz.q: The Epic of Gilgamesh is
ch: one of the oldest known written stories, about a king of Uruk

quiz.q: How did the wheel change Sumerian life?
ch: Carts could carry heavy loads, which helped trade and farming
It replaced the river for all travel

quiz.q: Sumerian sailboats were important because they

Explain why the invention of writing is considered a turning point in history.
quiz.ans: Writing let people keep records of trade, taxes and laws, pass on knowledge and stories, and it marks the beginning of written history, so we know far more about societies after writing.

practice.q: An empire is
ch: many lands and peoples ruled by one government or ruler
a single city with its own king

practice.h: His empire was called the Old Babylonian Empire.

practice.h: He united many cities under one ruler.

ch: so people could know the laws and their punishments
so only the king could read them
because paper had not been invented anywhere
practice.h: What good is a law if people do not know it?

practice.q: Hammurabi ruled from about 1792 BCE to about 1750 BCE. About how many years did he rule?
practice.h: For BCE dates, subtract the smaller number from the larger number.

practice.q: Read this law from Hammurabi's Code (translated by L. W. King, 1910): "If a man put out the eye of another man, his eye shall be put out." What idea of justice does this law show?
practice.ans: It shows the idea of "an eye for an eye": the punishment should match the crime, so the person suffers the same harm he caused.
practice.h: Compare the crime and the punishment.

quiz.q: Hammurabi's Code is important because it was one of the first

ch: to bring justice and protect weaker people
to make the strong more powerful

quiz.q: Law 53 says a man too lazy to keep his dam in good condition, whose broken dam floods the fields, must repay the crops destroyed. What does this law show about Babylon?
ch: Irrigation was so important that the law protected it

quiz.q: Under Hammurabi's Code, harming a noble brought a harsher penalty than harming an enslaved person. What does this show?
ch: Babylonian society had social classes that were not treated equally under the law
Everyone was equal under the law

quiz.q: Which statement compares Hammurabi's Code with laws in the United States today?
ch: Both are written down so people can know them, but U.S. law aims to treat all people equally

Both were carved on a stone pillar by a king

to stop the use of writing

quiz.q: Hammurabi said his laws came from the gods. Explain why linking laws to the gods might have helped him rule.
quiz.ans: If people believed the laws came from the gods, they would see the laws as fair and holy and be more likely to obey them and accept the king's authority.

test.ans: They provided water, fertile silt, fish and routes for trade, but their floods were unpredictable and could destroy crops and villages, and the dry climate required hard work building canals and levees.

test.q: Describe two achievements of the Sumerians and explain why each was important.
test.ans: Cuneiform let people keep records and write laws and stories; the wheel improved transportation and pottery making; the plow made farming easier; irrigation systems produced surplus food.

test.q: Source A: Hammurabi's prologue (translated by L. W. King, 1910) says he made his laws "to bring about the rule of righteousness in the land, to destroy the wicked and the evil-doers; so that the strong should not harm the weak." Source B: Law 196 says a man who puts out another man's eye shall have his eye put out, but Law 198 says if he puts out the eye of a freed man, he shall pay one gold mina. Make a claim about whether Hammurabi's Code protected everyone equally. Use evidence from both sources and explain your reasoning.
test.ans: Claim: Hammurabi's Code aimed for justice but did not protect everyone equally. units.name: Unit 3: Ancient Egypt and Kush (6.2)

lessons.name: The Nile River and Egyptian farming

practice.q: Ancient Egypt grew up along which river?
practice.h: It is one of the longest rivers in the world.

practice.q: The Nile flows from south to north. This means Upper Egypt was in the

practice.q: The fan-shaped area of rich land where the Nile meets the Mediterranean Sea is called the
practice.h: It is named after a Greek letter shaped like a triangle.

practice.q: What happened each year when the Nile flooded?
ch: It left a layer of dark, fertile silt on the fields
It washed all the soil into the sea
It turned the river into a desert
practice.h: Egyptians called their land Kemet, the "black land."

practice.q: A map shows the Nile with a scale of 1 centimeter = 200 kilometers. The river measures about 33 centimeters on the map. About how long is the Nile in kilometers?
practice.h: Multiply 33 by 200.

practice.q: The Greek historian Herodotus, writing about 440 BCE, called Egypt "the gift of the river" (adapted translation). Explain what he meant.
practice.ans: Without the Nile, Egypt would be desert. The river's floods brought water and rich soil for farming, and the river was used for travel and trade, so Egypt's whole civilization depended on it.
practice.h: What would Egypt be like without the Nile?

quiz.q: The deserts on both sides of the Nile Valley helped Egypt by

quiz.q: Egyptian farmers planted their crops

quiz.q: Why could Egyptian boats travel both ways on the Nile?
ch: The current carried boats north, and winds from the north pushed sails south
The river flowed in both directions

quiz.q: Which crops did Egyptian farmers grow in the rich soil?
Egyptians divided the year into 3 seasons of 4 months each, and each month had 30 days. How many days were in these 12 months?
A field produced 1,200 sacks of grain. The farmer paid 1 out of every 5 sacks as a tax to the pharaoh. How many sacks did the farmer pay?
Explain why most Egyptians lived on a narrow strip of land near the Nile.
quiz.ans: Most of Egypt is desert with little rain. Only the land near the river had water and fertile soil for farming, so people lived where they could grow food.

practice.q: The rulers of ancient Egypt were called
practice.h: The word first meant "great house."

practice.q: Egyptians believed their pharaoh was

practice.q: Why did Egyptians mummify the dead?
ch: They believed the body was needed in the afterlife

practice.q: Egyptian history is divided into the Old Kingdom (about 2686 to 2181 BCE), Middle Kingdom and New Kingdom. About how many years did the Old Kingdom last?
practice.h: Subtract the smaller BCE date from the larger one.

practice.ans: Pharaoh at the top; then priests and nobles; then scribes and government officials; then artisans and merchants; then farmers, the largest group; enslaved people at the bottom.
practice.h: Who had the most power, and which group had the most people?

ch: People believed obeying the pharaoh was a religious duty
It meant the pharaoh never needed officials
It kept the Nile from flooding

quiz.q: Compare the role of religion in the government of Egypt and of Mesopotamia.
quiz.ans: In both, rulers claimed support from the gods and temples were powerful. In Egypt, the pharaoh was seen as a god himself, while Mesopotamian kings were seen as servants or representatives of the gods.

practice.q: Egyptian writing that used picture symbols is called
practice.h: The word means "sacred carvings."

practice.q: Egyptians made a paper-like writing material from
practice.h: Our word "paper" comes from its name.

practice.h: Both dates are BCE. Subtract.

practice.ans: It suggests the pyramids were built by organized teams of paid and fed workers, including farmers who worked during the flood season, who lived nearby, ate well and were buried with honor.

quiz.q: Why did the Egyptians develop a calendar of 365 days?
ch: to predict the yearly flooding of the Nile

quiz.q: Building huge pyramids shows that the Old Kingdom had

quiz.q: Kush's later rulers sometimes included powerful queens known as
Why was Meroe a good location for iron-making?

quiz.ans: Kush was on the Nile between Egypt and central Africa, so goods like gold, ivory and ebony from the south passed through it. It also had gold mines and iron ore of its own.

quiz.q: Archaeologists found that Indus cities had streets laid out in a grid and covered drains. What does this show?
ch: The cities were carefully planned by a strong organized government
The cities grew without any plan
The cities were built by Greeks

quiz.q: The Indus Valley people used standard weights and bricks of the same size. Why was this useful?
ch: It made trade and building fair and consistent
It made writing easier to read
It kept the river from flooding

quiz.q: Why do historians still know less about the Indus Valley civilization than about Egypt?
ch: No one has yet been able to read the Indus script
The Indus people left no artifacts
The cities have never been found

quiz.q: Seals from the Indus Valley have been found in Mesopotamia. What can you conclude?
ch: The Indus Valley traded with Mesopotamia
The Indus Valley was ruled by Hammurabi
The seals were made in Egypt

quiz.q: Which natural feature helped protect the Indian subcontinent from invasion from the north?
Mohenjo-daro may have had about 40,000 people. If the average household had 8 people, about how many households were there?
Historians are not sure why the Indus cities declined after about 1900 BCE. Which explanation is supported by evidence of rivers changing course and dry soil?
ch: Changes in climate and rivers made farming harder
The cities were flooded by the Atlantic
The people moved to the Americas

quiz.q: Compare the Indus Valley cities with Sumerian cities. Give one similarity and one difference.
quiz.ans: Similarity: both grew along rivers, had trade, writing and planned buildings. Difference: Indus cities had grid streets and advanced drainage, and their writing has not been deciphered, while Sumerian cuneiform can be read.

lessons.name: Vedic society and the beliefs of Hinduism

practice.q: The oldest sacred texts of Hinduism, composed in Sanskrit, are the
practice.h: Their name means "knowledge."

practice.q: In Vedic society, people were divided into four main social groups called
practice.h: These groups became the basis of the caste system.

practice.q: Which list shows the four varnas from the highest to lowest rank in Vedic society?
practice.h: Priests were at the top.

practice.q: The Hindu belief that the soul is reborn into a new body after death is called
practice.h: The cycle of birth, death and rebirth.

practice.q: The Rig Veda contains about 1,000 hymns divided into 10 books. If each book had the same number of hymns, how many hymns would each book have?
practice.h: Divide 1,000 by 10.

practice.q: Explain what the Hindu ideas of dharma and karma mean and how they are connected.
practice.ans: Dharma is a person's duty according to their place in life. Karma is the idea that a person's actions bring results in this life or future lives. Fulfilling one's dharma brings good karma and a better rebirth.
practice.h: One idea is about duty; the other is about the results of actions.

quiz.q: Many Hindus believe in a single universal spirit that is the source of all things, called
In Hinduism, moksha is
ch: freedom from the cycle of rebirth

quiz.q: Which group was at the top of the varna system and performed religious ceremonies?
How did the caste system affect daily life in ancient India?
ch: It decided a person's job, whom they could marry and how they were treated
It had no effect on daily life
It let people change groups whenever they wished

quiz.q: Some people outside the four varnas did jobs considered unclean and were treated very unfairly. What does this show about ancient Indian society?
ch: It had a rigid hierarchy with deep inequality

quiz.q: Indo-Aryan peoples began moving into northern India about 1500 BCE. The Indus cities had declined by about 1900 BCE. About how many years apart were these events?
According to karma, which would most likely lead to a better rebirth?
ch: carrying out one's duties honestly and treating others well
breaking the rules of one's group

quiz.q: Explain how the beliefs in karma and reincarnation may have encouraged people to accept the caste system.
quiz.ans: People believed their place in life came from actions in past lives, and that doing their duty would bring a better rebirth, so they were encouraged to accept their position rather than challenge it.

practice.q: The founder of Buddhism was
practice.h: He was a prince who gave up his wealth.

practice.q: The title "Buddha" means
practice.h: Think about what he reached under the tree.

practice.q: According to Buddhist tradition, Siddhartha left his palace after seeing an old man, a sick man and a dead man. Why did these sights trouble him?
ch: They showed him that all people suffer, even the rich
He had never seen anyone working
He wanted to become a soldier
He was afraid of the monsoon
practice.h: What do old age, sickness and death have in common?

practice.q: The Buddha taught the Middle Way, which means
ch: avoiding both too much luxury and too much self-denial
living only in the middle of cities
eating only one meal a day
practice.h: He had tried both extremes.

practice.q: The Buddha's teachings include the Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path. How many teachings are in these two lists combined?
practice.h: Add 4 and 8.

practice.q: Read this verse from the Dhammapada, a collection of Buddhist teachings (translated by F. Max Muller, 1881): "For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love, this is an old rule." Explain this teaching in your own words.
practice.ans: Answering hate with more hate only keeps it going. Hatred ends only when people respond with love and kindness.
practice.h: What happens when two people keep hurting each other?

quiz.q: The final goal of Buddhism, a state of peace and freedom from suffering, is called
According to the Four Noble Truths, what is the cause of suffering?
How was Buddhism different from the Vedic religion of its time?
ch: It taught that anyone could reach enlightenment, regardless of varna
It required priests to perform every ritual
It worshipped many gods of nature

quiz.q: Buddhism spread from India to places such as Sri Lanka, China and Southeast Asia mainly through
Which is part of the Eightfold Path?
Many historians date the Buddha's life to about 480 BCE to 400 BCE. Using these dates, how long did he live?
Why might people of lower varnas have been attracted to Buddhism?
ch: It taught that all people could reach enlightenment, which offered hope beyond their social rank
It gave them land and money
It required them to stay in their varna

quiz.q: Source A: The Buddha taught that suffering comes from desire and that people can end suffering by following the Eightfold Path. Source B: Buddhist monasteries welcomed people from all social groups, and the Buddha taught in everyday language instead of Sanskrit. Make a claim about why Buddhism attracted many followers. Use evidence from both sources and explain your reasoning.
quiz.ans: Claim: Buddhism attracted many followers because it offered all people a practical way to end suffering. Evidence: Source A shows the Buddha taught a clear path, the Eightfold Path, to end suffering. Source B shows monasteries welcomed all social groups and the Buddha used everyday language. Reasoning: A path that anyone could follow and teachings that ordinary people could understand opened Buddhism to people whom the varna system kept from full religious roles.

Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.

practice.q: The first great empire to unite most of the Indian subcontinent was the
practice.h: It was founded by Chandragupta Maurya about 321 BCE.

practice.q: After the bloody conquest of Kalinga, the emperor Ashoka
ch: became a Buddhist and promised to rule through peace and kindness
practice.h: He was horrified by the deaths in the war.

practice.q: Ashoka spread his ideas by
ch: carving edicts on rocks and pillars across his empire
practice.h: Some of these stone carvings still stand today.

practice.q: The Gupta Empire is known as a golden age because of
ch: great achievements in mathematics, science, art and literature
practice.h: Golden age means a time of peace and great accomplishment.

practice.q: Ashoka ruled from about 268 BCE to about 232 BCE. About how many years did he rule?
practice.h: Subtract the BCE dates.

practice.q: Ashoka's edicts (adapted translation) say that he felt deep sorrow over the many people killed and taken away in the Kalinga war. How did this change the way he ruled?
practice.ans: He turned to Buddhism, gave up wars of conquest, and promoted nonviolence, respect for all religions, care for the sick and kindness to people and animals.
practice.h: What did he do differently after the war?

quiz.q: Indian mathematicians of the Gupta period helped develop
ch: the decimal place-value system and the use of zero

quiz.q: The astronomer Aryabhata, born in 476 CE, taught that
ch: the Earth rotates on its axis
the Sun goes around a flat Earth
the Moon makes its own light

ch: It improved trade, travel and communication

ch: He asked people to respect all religions
He ordered everyone to become Hindu

quiz.q: The Gupta Empire began about 320 CE and lasted until about 550 CE. About how many years did it last?
Which best explains why Indian numerals spread to Southwest Asia and Europe?
ch: Traders and scholars carried them along trade routes, and Arab mathematicians adopted them
They were carved on the pyramids

quiz.q: Explain why the decimal system with zero was an important contribution to the world.
quiz.ans: Place value with zero made arithmetic much easier than with Roman numerals and allowed advances in math, science, trade and today's computers.

making all of India a desert

The Buddha taught that suffering could be ended by

ch: Monks, missionaries and merchants carried it along trade routes to other parts of Asia
Roman soldiers spread it to Europe
It was carved on the Rosetta Stone

test.q: Chandragupta Maurya founded his empire about 321 BCE. Ashoka began to rule about 268 BCE. About how many years later did Ashoka begin to rule?
Aryabhata was born in 476 CE. How many years ago was that from 2026?
Ashoka issued 14 Major Rock Edicts and 7 Major Pillar Edicts. How many times as many Major Rock Edicts as Major Pillar Edicts did he issue?

ch: Both teach reincarnation and karma, but Buddhism taught that anyone could reach enlightenment regardless of varna
Buddhism rejects all ideas from Hinduism

test.q: Why might Ashoka have asked his people to respect all religions?
ch: His empire included many religious groups, and tolerance helped keep peace and unity
He wanted to end all religion

test.q: Which source would be a primary source about the Maurya Empire?
ch: a modern textbook chapter on India
a website summarizing the Gupta Empire

test.q: Which list is in the correct chronological order?
ch: Indus cities flourish, Vedic period begins, Maurya Empire, Gupta Empire
Gupta Empire, Maurya Empire, Indus cities flourish, Vedic period begins
Maurya Empire, Indus cities flourish, Gupta Empire, Vedic period begins
Vedic period begins, Gupta Empire, Indus cities flourish, Maurya Empire

test.q: Explain how the varna system shaped people's lives in ancient India.
test.ans: A person was born into a varna that largely decided their job, who they could marry and how they were treated; Brahmins had the highest status, and people outside the varnas faced harsh discrimination.

test.q: Describe two achievements of ancient India that still affect the world today.
test.ans: The decimal system with zero is used everywhere; Buddhism and Hinduism are major world religions; Aryabhata's astronomy; yoga and literature such as the Vedas and epics.

test.q: Source A (Ashoka's Rock Edict 13, about 256 BCE, adapted translation): After the conquest of Kalinga, Ashoka wrote that he felt deep remorse for the many people killed and carried away, and that he now wished to win people over by dharma (right conduct) rather than by war. Source B: Ashoka built roads with shade trees and wells, set up places to care for sick people and animals, and sent Buddhist teachers to other lands. Make a claim about how Buddhism affected Ashoka's rule. Use evidence from both sources and explain your reasoning.
test.ans: Claim: Buddhism changed Ashoka from a conqueror into a ruler who focused on peace and the welfare of his people. Evidence: Source A shows he felt remorse after the Kalinga war and chose to rule by right conduct instead of war. Source B shows he built roads, wells and places to care for the sick and sent Buddhist teachers abroad. Reasoning: Buddhist teachings of nonviolence and compassion explain why he stopped conquest and used his power to help people and spread his beliefs.
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.

units.name: Unit 7: Ancient China (6.6)
units.el: Use a physical map of China with the Huang He, Chang Jiang, Gobi Desert and Himalayas, and a dynasty timeline strip (Shang, Zhou, Qin, Han). Pre-teach dynasty, Mandate of Heaven, filial piety, Legalism, standardize and Silk Road; give a three-column chart for Confucianism, Daoism and Legalism.

lessons.name: Geography and the Shang and Zhou dynasties

practice.q: Chinese civilization began along the
practice.h: The river is named for the color of the soil it carries.

practice.q: A dynasty is
ch: a series of rulers from the same family
practice.h: The Shang, Zhou and Han are examples.

practice.q: The Huang He was called "China's Sorrow" because
ch: its floods often destroyed villages and killed many people
no one could farm near it
practice.h: The river brought both rich soil and disaster.

practice.q: How did deserts, mountains and the Pacific Ocean affect ancient China?
ch: They isolated China, so it developed its own culture with less outside contact
They made China part of Mesopotamia
They connected China closely to Greece
practice.h: Look at what lies on each side of China.

practice.q: The Shang dynasty lasted from about 1600 BCE to 1046 BCE. About how many years did it last?
practice.h: Subtract 1046 from 1600.

practice.q: Shang kings asked questions about the future by carving them on animal bones or turtle shells and heating them until they cracked. What can historians learn from these oracle bones?
practice.ans: They contain the earliest Chinese writing and show what Shang rulers worried about, such as harvests, weather, wars and illness, and how they tried to learn the will of their ancestors and gods.
practice.h: Think about the writing on the bones and the questions it asks.

quiz.q: The fine yellow soil carried by the Huang He is called
The Zhou rulers claimed the right to rule through the
According to the Mandate of Heaven, what showed that a dynasty had lost heaven's approval?
ch: floods, famines, rebellions and other disasters

quiz.q: The Shang dynasty is known for its skill in making
Under Zhou feudalism, the king gave land to
ch: lords who promised loyalty and soldiers in return

quiz.q: The Zhou dynasty lasted from 1046 BCE to 256 BCE. How many years did it last?
How could the Mandate of Heaven be used to justify a rebellion?
ch: Rebels could claim that disasters proved the ruler had lost heaven's approval
It said rulers could never be replaced

quiz.q: Explain how the Mandate of Heaven helped explain the dynastic cycle in Chinese history.
quiz.ans: A new dynasty claimed heaven's approval; over time rulers grew weak or unjust, disasters and revolts followed, and a new family claimed the Mandate and founded the next dynasty, and the cycle repeated.

practice.q: Confucius was a teacher who lived from about 551 to 479 BCE. His sayings were collected in the
practice.h: His students wrote down his teachings.

practice.q: Confucius taught that society would be orderly if
ch: people respected their roles in five key relationships, such as ruler and subject and parent and child
practice.h: Think about family and duty.

practice.q: Filial piety means
ch: respect and care for one's parents and ancestors
practice.h: Filial refers to sons and daughters.

practice.q: Daoism, linked to the teacher Laozi, teaches people to
ch: live simply and in harmony with nature and the Dao (the Way)
follow strict laws with harsh punishments
practice.h: The Dao means "the Way."

practice.q: The Warring States period lasted from 475 BCE to 221 BCE. How many years was that?
practice.h: Subtract the smaller BCE date from the larger.

practice.q: Confucius said (Analects, translated by James Legge, 1861): "What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others." Explain this teaching and give an example of following it.
practice.ans: Treat other people the way you want to be treated. For example, if you do not want people to make fun of you, do not make fun of others.
practice.h: Think of a time someone treated you in a way you did not like.

quiz.q: Legalism taught that people should be controlled by
Confucius believed rulers should govern mainly by
Why did Confucianism, Daoism and Legalism develop during the Warring States period?
ch: Thinkers were searching for ways to bring order to a time of war and chaos
China was peaceful and had no problems
Rome asked China for new ideas

quiz.q: Which statement would a Daoist most likely make?
ch: "Do not struggle against the natural flow of life."
"Obey your king in all things because he is a god."

quiz.q: Which pair is correctly matched?
ch: Confucianism, harmony with nature above all

quiz.q: Confucius was born in 551 BCE and died in 479 BCE. How old was he when he died? (Subtract the dates.)

Confucius said (Analects, translated by James Legge, 1861) that if people are led by laws and punishments, "they will try to avoid the punishment, but have no sense of shame." Which belief system did this statement challenge?

Source A (Confucius, Analects, translated by James Legge, 1861): "If they be led by virtue... they will have the sense of shame, and moreover will become good." Source B: Legalist thinkers argued that people are selfish by nature and will obey only if laws are strict and punishments are harsh. Make a claim about how Confucianism and Legalism differed in their view of people and government. Use evidence from both sources and explain your reasoning.
quiz.ans: Claim: Confucianism trusted that people could become good through example, while Legalism believed people must be forced to obey. Evidence: Source A says people led by virtue will feel shame and become good. Source B says Legalists thought people were selfish and would obey only harsh laws. Reasoning: Because Confucius thought people could learn goodness, he wanted rulers to lead by example; because Legalists thought people were selfish, they wanted rulers to control them with fear.
rub: Clear, accurate claim; relevant and sufficient evidence; reasoning that explains how the evidence supports the claim using key ideas from the unit.
Accurate claim and relevant evidence; the reasoning is only partly explained.
A claim with limited or partly relevant evidence and little reasoning.
The claim is unclear or inaccurate, with little or no evidence or reasoning.

practice.q: The ruler who unified China in 221 BCE and called himself the First Emperor was
practice.h: The name China may come from his dynasty's name.

practice.q: Qin Shi Huangdi ruled using the ideas of
practice.h: He used strict laws and harsh punishments.

practice.q: To unify China, the First Emperor standardized
practice.h: Standardize means to make the same everywhere.

practice.q: Why did Qin Shi Huangdi connect and extend earlier walls into a long wall in the north?
ch: to defend China against attacks by nomadic peoples
to keep the Huang He from flooding
to mark the border with India
to hold back the Pacific Ocean
practice.h: Who lived to the north of China?

practice.q: Qin Shi Huangdi unified China in 221 BCE and died in 210 BCE. How many years did he rule all of China?
practice.h: Subtract the BCE dates.

practice.q: Explain why having one standard system of writing helped unify China.
practice.ans: People in different regions spoke different languages, but with one writing system officials could send orders, collect taxes and keep records everywhere, and people could share ideas.
practice.h: How would officials communicate with distant regions?

quiz.q: In 1974, farmers digging a well near Xi'an discovered
ch: thousands of life-size clay soldiers in the First Emperor's tomb complex

quiz.q: Why did many people resent the Qin dynasty?
ch: It forced people into hard labor, raised taxes and punished critics harshly
It gave everyone too much freedom
It made Confucianism the official belief

quiz.q: The First Emperor ordered many books burned because
ch: he wanted to stop people from criticizing his rule with old ideas
the books were too heavy to store
the books were written in Greek

quiz.q: Standard axle widths for carts in the Qin dynasty helped
ch: carts travel easily on roads across the empire

quiz.q: Which is an effect of the Qin dynasty that lasted long after it fell?
ch: a unified China with a standard writing system

quiz.q: The Qin dynasty began in 221 BCE and fell in 206 BCE. How many years did it last?
Which evidence best supports the claim that the First Emperor had enormous power?
ch: His tomb complex included an army of thousands of clay soldiers built by many workers

quiz.q: Was the First Emperor a successful ruler? Give one argument for and one argument against.
quiz.ans: For: he unified China, standardized writing, money and measures, and built roads and walls. Against: he ruled harshly, burned books, punished critics and forced people into labor, and his dynasty fell only four years after he died.

lessons.name: The Han dynasty and the Silk Road

practice.q: The dynasty that ruled China from 206 BCE to 220 CE is the
practice.h: Many Chinese people still call themselves by this dynasty's name.

practice.q: Han emperors made Confucianism the official belief of the government and
ch: began choosing some officials by examinations on Confucian learning
practice.h: Officials needed to know Confucius' teachings.

practice.q: Which invention of the Han dynasty changed how people recorded information?
ch: the printing press with movable metal type
practice.h: Before this, Chinese people wrote on bamboo strips and silk.

practice.q: The Silk Road was
ch: a network of trade routes linking China with Central Asia, India, Persia and the Mediterranean
a single paved road in Rome
a wall built by the Han
practice.h: It was named for China's most famous export.

practice.q: The Silk Road stretched about 6,400 kilometers. A caravan traveled about 32 kilometers a day. About how many days would it take to travel the whole route without stopping?
practice.h: Divide the total distance by the distance each day.

practice.q: Explain how the Silk Road spread both goods and ideas.
practice.ans: Merchants carried silk, paper and other goods west and brought horses, glass and new foods east. Along the way, ideas and religions such as Buddhism spread into China.
practice.h: Traders carried more than things to sell.

quiz.q: Emperor Wudi sent the explorer Zhang Qian west in 138 BCE. What was one result of his travels?
ch: Han China learned about lands to the west, which helped open the Silk Road

quiz.q: Why did the Chinese keep the way they made silk a secret?
ch: Silk was very valuable, and controlling it brought China great wealth
Silk could only be made in Rome

quiz.q: Which religion entered China from India along the Silk Road during the Han dynasty?
During the Han dynasty, Zhang Heng built an instrument that
ch: detected the direction of distant earthquakes
told time by the stars only

quiz.q: The Han dynasty lasted from 206 BCE to 220 CE. Counting the years before and after year 1 separately and adding them, about how many years did it last?
Why did the civil service examination system matter?
ch: It meant some government jobs went to educated people chosen by tests, not only to nobles
It gave all jobs to soldiers

quiz.q: A Roman writer complained that Roman women spent too much money on silk. What does this suggest?
ch: Chinese silk reached Rome through Silk Road trade and was highly valued
Rome made all of its own silk

quiz.q: Compare the Qin and Han dynasties' ways of governing.
quiz.ans: The Qin used Legalism, harsh laws and forced labor, and lasted only 15 years. The Han kept a strong central government but used Confucian ideas and educated officials, and lasted about 400 years.

test.q: According to the Mandate of Heaven, a ruler could lose the right to rule if
ch: he ruled unjustly and disasters struck

test.q: Which belief system taught people to live in harmony with nature and the Dao?
Which belief system did Qin Shi Huangdi use to rule?
Which was an accomplishment of the Qin dynasty?
ch: standardizing writing, money, weights and measures

test.q: Which was an achievement of the Han dynasty?
Under the Han, officials were increasingly chosen based on
ch: knowledge of Confucian teachings tested by examinations

test.q: Which good did China export along the Silk Road?
The Shang dynasty began about 1600 BCE. The Qin unified China in 221 BCE. About how many years apart were these events?
The Han dynasty began in 206 BCE. Zhang Qian set out on his journey west in 138 BCE. How many years after the Han began was that?

ch: His harsh laws, high taxes and forced labor led to rebellions

test.q: Which statement best compares Confucianism and Legalism?
ch: Confucianism stressed moral example and duty, while Legalism stressed strict laws and punishment

Legalism stressed kindness and Confucianism stressed fear

test.q: How did the Silk Road change China?
ch: It brought new goods, ideas and religions such as Buddhism into China
It cut China off from the world
It ended the Han dynasty right away

test.q: Which list is in the correct chronological order?

test.ans: He conquered the warring states, ruled with Legalist laws, standardized writing, coins, weights and measures, built roads, and connected walls to defend the north.

test.q: Explain two ways Confucianism shaped government in Han China.
test.ans: It became the official belief, so rulers were expected to set a moral example; officials were chosen by examinations on Confucian texts; respect for family and order shaped laws.

test.q: Source A (Confucius, Analects, translated by James Legge, 1861): "What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others." Source B: Han emperors made Confucianism the official teaching, founded an imperial academy to teach Confucian texts, and chose some officials by examining their knowledge of these texts. units.name: Unit 8: Ancient Rome (6.7)
units.el: Use a map of the Mediterranean that shows Rome's growth in colors, and a chart that matches parts of the Roman Republic to the U.S. government (consuls, Senate, tribunes). practice.q: Rome was built on seven hills beside the
practice.h: This river runs through central Italy to the sea.

practice.ans: After living under kings, Romans did not want one person to hold too much power. Two consuls could check each other, and short terms kept leaders from becoming tyrants.
practice.h: What were the Romans afraid of?

quiz.q: In the early Roman Republic, the wealthy landowning families who held most power were called

ch: common people such as farmers, artisans and merchants

quiz.q: The Senate in the Roman Republic
ch: advised the consuls and controlled government money and foreign policy

was made up of plebeians only

ch: vetoing actions of the government that harmed them

soc|12.about: Twelfth grade studies Principles of American Democracy and Economics: the foundations of the Constitution, rights and the Supreme Court, political participation and elections, and how markets, government and the global economy work.
std: Students explain the fundamental principles and moral values of American democracy as expressed in the U.S. Constitution and other essential documents.
Students evaluate and take and defend positions on the scope and limits of rights and obligations as democratic citizens.
Students summarize landmark U.S. Supreme Court interpretations of the Constitution and its amendments.
Students evaluate issues regarding campaigns for national, state and local elective offices.
Students understand common economic terms and concepts and economic reasoning.
Students analyze the influence of the federal government on the American economy.
